domains.name: Revising, Editing & Proofreading
domains.summary: Covers how writers improve drafts: distinguishing revision of argument and structure from sentence-level editing and surface proofreading, and the techniques, feedback sources, tools and ethical limits involved. Sommers (1980) found that inexperienced writers tend to treat revision as rewording, so teaching should put global revision and criteria-based self-assessment before editing. The value of written corrective feedback has been contested (Truscott, 1996; Ferris, 1999), but meta-analytic evidence suggests it can improve accuracy (Kang & Han, 2015); learners therefore need routines for targeted self-editing, trained peer review (Lundstrom & Baker, 2009) and critical use of tools and permitted third-party help.
domains.learnerSummary: You will learn how to improve your drafts in stages—first the argument and structure, then the sentences, then surface errors—and how to use marking criteria, classmates' feedback, digital tools and proofreaders appropriately.

stageEmphasis.foundation: Establish the difference between revising and correcting, basic self-editing routines and structured, supported peer review.
stageEmphasis.pre-sessional: Build multi-draft cycles with criteria-based self-assessment, peer review and targeted editing of personal error patterns.
stageEmphasis.in-sessional-ug: Apply revision strategies to module assignments and use tools and proofreading support within institutional rules.
stageEmphasis.in-sessional-pgt: Focus on efficient global revision under time pressure and on critical use of editing and AI tools.
stageEmphasis.pgr: Revise long texts with reverse outlining and supervisor and peer feedback, edit for style at publication level, and understand the rules on editorial help with theses and articles.

domains.name: Essay Construction
domains.summary: Covers how an essay is built around a central argument: structure, thesis, introductions, body organisation, conclusions, relevance to the question, essay types, depth of focus, criticality, headings and titles. The essay is a major assessed genre in many humanities and social science programmes but is only one of many genre families in university writing (Nesi & Gardner, 2012), and the five-paragraph essay taught in many schools and test-preparation courses is a scaffold that does not match university essays in length, structure or source use (Caplan & Johns, 2019; Moore & Morton, 2005). Teaching should centre on argument (Wingate, 2012) and treat structural templates as means to that end.
domains.learnerSummary: You will learn how to plan and build an essay that answers the question with a clear, well-supported and critical argument, from the thesis and introduction through the body to the conclusion and title.

stageEmphasis.foundation: Introduce thesis-led essay structure with scaffolds, moving from short opinion-based essays to short source-based ones.
stageEmphasis.pre-sessional: Develop extended source-based essays with a clear thesis, organised body and evaluative conclusion, and unlearn test-driven templates.
stageEmphasis.in-sessional-ug: Work with disciplinary essay types, answering the specific question, choosing depth over breadth and demonstrating criticality.
stageEmphasis.in-sessional-pgt: Focus on criticality, scope and argument in short, dense essays and on discipline-specific conventions such as headings.
stageEmphasis.pgr: Carry argument structure and title-writing skills into articles and thesis chapters; essays themselves are less central.

domains.name: Paragraph Development
domains.summary: Covers the paragraph as the main unit through which academic writers develop and support a point: controlling ideas, support and analysis, internal coherence, closure, division, paragraph functions and the integration of sources. Paragraph scaffolds such as topic-sentence models and PEEL are useful entry points for foundation and pre-sessional writers, but expert paragraphs vary considerably (Braddock, 1974), so teaching should move learners from templates towards functional judgements about what a paragraph needs to do in its context. Coherence is better taught through information flow and logical relations than through connector lists (Crossley & McNamara, 2012).
domains.learnerSummary: You will learn how to build paragraphs that make one clear point, support it with explanation and evidence, flow logically from sentence to sentence, use sources while keeping your own voice, and connect to the rest of your text.

stageEmphasis.foundation: Build secure control of the controlling idea, support and closure, using scaffolds such as PEEL explicitly as temporary supports.
stageEmphasis.pre-sessional: Shift to source-based paragraphs in which the writer's own point leads and evidence is integrated and commented on.
stageEmphasis.in-sessional-ug: Diagnose paragraph-level problems in disciplinary assignments, especially description without analysis and breaks in internal coherence.
stageEmphasis.in-sessional-pgt: Focus on dense, multi-source paragraphs and on flexible paragraphing that serves the argument rather than a formula.

domains.name: Writing Process
domains.summary: Covers how academic texts are produced rather than what they look like: representing the task, generating and organising content, drafting, writing from sources, and managing time, language choice and affect across extended projects. It draws on cognitive process models (Flower & Hayes, 1981; Bereiter & Scardamalia, 1987) and L2 composing research (Zamel, 1983), which show that skilled writers plan, draft and review recursively and use writing to develop ideas. Hyland (2003) argues that process pedagogy needs to be complemented by explicit attention to genre and reader expectations, so these topics should be taught alongside PAR, ESS and the genre strands rather than as a free-standing ‘process approach’.
domains.learnerSummary: You will learn how to turn an assignment brief into a plan and a draft, how to use your reading and your other languages while you write, and how to manage longer projects and the times when writing feels stuck.

stageEmphasis.foundation: Make the process visible: task analysis, idea generation and outlining for short assignments, with plans and drafts submitted and discussed before the final text.
stageEmphasis.pre-sessional: Use the extended source-based project to rehearse the full cycle under realistic deadlines, including reading-to-write, word budgeting and drafting from notes.
stageEmphasis.in-sessional-ug: Apply process strategies to learners' own module assignments, with emphasis on interpreting briefs, juggling deadlines and integrating disciplinary reading.
stageEmphasis.in-sessional-pgt: Compress the cycle for dense, short-turnaround master's assignments and plan ahead for the dissertation.
stageEmphasis.pgr: Treat writing as a way of thinking and as sustained practice: routines, milestones, writing blocks and plurilingual composing across a multi-year project.

topics.name: Revision, editing and proofreading
topics.description: Distinguish three levels of work on a draft—revision (changing argument, content and structure), editing (improving sentences for clarity, accuracy and style) and proofreading (correcting surface errors in the final version)—and sequence them so that effort is not spent polishing text that may later be cut. The distinction underpins efficient self-review, well-targeted feedback requests and institutional rules on third-party help.
masteryEvidence: Classifies given changes to a draft as revision, editing or proofreading
Sequences work on a draft from global to local and explains why
Requests feedback appropriate to the stage of the draft
Explains how the distinction relates to what a proofreader may and may not change
topics.assessmentPrompt: Show ten changes between two drafts (a moved paragraph, a new counter-argument, a reworded sentence, a corrected article, a fixed typing error, and so on). Ask the learner to classify them and say which kinds should be done first. Check that they recognise structural and content changes as revision and prioritise them.

topics.name: Global revision
topics.description: Revise a draft at whole-text level by re-examining the thesis, the line of argument, the selection and sufficiency of evidence, the order of sections and the fit with the task and reader, and make substantial changes—adding, cutting, moving or rewriting sections—where needed. Global revision usually improves a text far more than sentence-level correction does.
masteryEvidence: Identifies the most important global problem in a draft, such as a thesis–body mismatch or a missing counter-argument
Makes structural changes (moving, cutting, adding sections) and explains how they improve the argument
Revises the thesis to match what the draft argues, or the body to match the thesis
Uses feedback on content and structure to plan specific revisions
Rereads a draft from the perspective of its intended reader and acts on what that reveals
topics.assessmentPrompt: Give a draft whose thesis promises an evaluation but whose body only describes. Ask the learner what the main problem is and to plan the revision. Check that they identify the global mismatch and propose structural or content changes rather than sentence edits.

topics.name: Reverse outlining
topics.description: Test the structure of a draft by writing a one-line statement of each paragraph's point (and, optionally, its function), then reading the statements in sequence to find gaps, repetition, misplaced paragraphs, paragraphs with more than one point and mismatches with the thesis. The technique turns a vague sense that ‘something is wrong’ into specific revision decisions.
masteryEvidence: Writes an accurate one-line statement of the point of each paragraph in a draft
Identifies from the outline paragraphs with no clear point or with more than one point
Detects repetition, gaps and illogical order from the outline
Uses the outline to plan specific revisions and checks the revised draft with a new outline
topics.assessmentPrompt: Ask the learner to reverse-outline a 1,000-word draft (their own or supplied) and list three revisions the outline suggests. Check that the paragraph statements are accurate claims rather than topics, and that the proposed revisions are structural.

topics.name: Editing for style and clarity
topics.description: Edit sentences to make them clearer, more concise and appropriate in register—bringing subjects and verbs together, reducing wordiness and redundancy, managing information density, choosing precise vocabulary and revising informal or vague expressions—while preserving meaning and the writer's voice. Style editing follows global revision and precedes proofreading.
masteryEvidence: Identifies and revises unclear sentences (buried or distant subject and verb, ambiguous reference)
Removes redundancy and empty phrases without losing meaning
Revises informal or vague expressions to suit the register of the genre
Balances concision with readability, unpacking over-dense noun phrases where the reader needs it
Explains the reason for each edit
topics.assessmentPrompt: Give a 120-word paragraph containing wordiness, an informal phrase, a vague general noun and an over-dense sentence. Ask the learner to edit it and explain each change. Check that meaning is preserved and that edits target clarity and precision rather than inflating vocabulary.

topics.name: Editing for grammatical accuracy
topics.description: Edit drafts for grammatical accuracy by targeting one's own recurrent error types (for example articles, subject–verb agreement, tense, sentence boundaries) in focused passes, using feedback history, reference resources and personal checklists, rather than reading once for ‘all errors’. Targeted self-editing is more efficient than undirected checking and builds independence from teacher correction.
masteryEvidence: Names their three to five most frequent error types, using evidence from feedback history
Edits a draft in separate passes, each for a single error type
Finds and corrects most instances of a targeted error type in their own text
Checks uncertain forms in a grammar reference, learner dictionary or corpus
Tracks the frequency of targeted errors across drafts to monitor progress
topics.assessmentPrompt: Give the learner a previously corrected text and a new draft. Ask them to name their main error types and then edit the new draft for one of them in five minutes. Compare the instances they find and correct with the instances present.

topics.name: Proofreading
topics.description: Check a final version for surface errors—spelling, typing errors, punctuation, missing or repeated words, formatting, and consistency of spelling variety, terms and numbers—using techniques that counter the tendency to read what one meant rather than what is on the page, such as reading aloud, changing the font or layout, reading in reverse order for spelling, and using a checklist. Proofreading is the last stage, after revision and editing.
masteryEvidence: Proofreads using at least two techniques that change how the text is perceived
Detects and corrects most planted surface errors in a short text within a time limit
Checks consistency of spelling variety, terminology, numbers and formatting across a document
Leaves proofreading until revision and editing are complete
topics.assessmentPrompt: Give a 250-word text with ten planted surface errors (misspellings, wrong homophones, a missing word, mixed British and American spelling, punctuation). Allow five minutes. Count the errors found and ask which techniques the learner used.

topics.name: Self-assessing drafts against criteria
topics.description: Use marking criteria, rubrics, checklists and exemplars to judge the quality of one's own draft, identify the gap between current and target performance, and plan the revisions most likely to close it. Developing this evaluative judgement is central to becoming an independent writer and to making good use of feedback.
masteryEvidence: Translates each marking criterion into questions to ask of their own draft
Points to evidence in their draft to justify a judgement against each criterion
Makes self-assessments that broadly agree with a tutor's assessment of the same draft
Identifies the one or two changes most likely to move the draft into a higher band
Compares their draft with an exemplar and names specific differences
topics.assessmentPrompt: Before submission, ask the learner to self-assess a draft against a three-criterion rubric, giving a band and quoting evidence for each. Compare with tutor marking. Check for evidence-based judgements and accurate identification of the main weakness, not just the overall grade.

topics.name: Peer review of drafts
topics.description: Give specific, criteria-referenced and constructive feedback on a peer's draft, prioritising global issues, and receive and evaluate peer feedback, deciding what to act on. Reviewing others' writing also develops the reviewer's own evaluative judgement and revision skills.
masteryEvidence: Gives feedback that identifies specific strengths and the most important problems, with reasons and suggestions
Prioritises argument and organisation over surface errors when reviewing early drafts
Phrases critical comments in a mitigated, collegial way
Evaluates comments received and explains which to accept or reject
Applies insights gained from reviewing others to their own draft
topics.assessmentPrompt: Give a short draft with one serious global problem and several local errors; ask for written peer comments in ten minutes. Check whether the global problem is identified first, whether comments are specific and actionable, and whether the tone is constructive.

topics.name: Using editing tools critically
topics.description: Use spelling and grammar checkers, automated writing evaluation, readability measures and AI-based rewriting tools critically: knowing what they detect well and poorly, evaluating each suggestion against one's own knowledge and reference sources, and staying within institutional rules on permitted assistance. Tools can support accuracy but can also introduce errors, change meaning, flatten the writer's voice and, if over-used, raise integrity concerns.
masteryEvidence: Accepts or rejects tool suggestions with reasons, checking uncertain ones in a reference source
Identifies kinds of error that tools commonly miss or introduce
Explains why readability scores are not measures of academic quality
States the local rules on automated and AI tools in assessed work and complies with them
Keeps a record of tool use where disclosure is required
topics.assessmentPrompt: Give a paragraph with the suggestions a grammar checker produced for it, some correct, some wrong and one that changes the meaning. Ask the learner to accept or reject each. Check the accuracy of their decisions and whether rejections are justified.

topics.name: Acceptable third-party proofreading
topics.description: Understand institutional policies on proofreading and editing by third parties (friends, paid proofreaders, editors, AI tools): which kinds of change are typically permitted (surface errors, formatting consistency) and prohibited (rewriting content, argument or structure), what must be disclosed, and how editorial support for theses and publications differs from that permitted for assessed coursework. Crossing these limits can constitute misconduct even when help is well intended.
masteryEvidence: Summarises their institution's proofreading policy and says where it is published
Classifies proposed third-party changes as permitted or not under a given policy
Explains why substantive rewriting by another person can count as misconduct
Describes how to brief a proofreader within the rules and record what was changed
Distinguishes the editorial support norms for theses and journal articles from those for coursework
topics.assessmentPrompt: Give five changes a proofreader made to a student essay (corrected spelling, rewrote a paragraph, added a reference, restructured the argument, standardised formatting). Ask which are permitted under a supplied sample policy. Check the classifications and the reasons given.

topics.name: Academic essay structure
topics.description: Understand how an essay's introduction, body and conclusion relate to a central argument: the introduction frames the question and states the position, the body develops it through a sequence of supported points, and the conclusion draws the argument together. Structure serves the argument, so the number, order and length of sections follow from the line of reasoning rather than from a fixed template.
masteryEvidence: Explains the role of the introduction, body and conclusion in relation to the essay's central argument
Maps the argument of a model essay by stating each body paragraph's point and how it advances the thesis
Distinguishes a university essay from a five-paragraph test essay in length, organisation and use of sources
Plans an essay whose number and order of sections follow from the argument rather than from a template
topics.assessmentPrompt: Show an outline for a ‘to what extent’ question that consists of three advantages, three disadvantages and a conclusion. Ask what the problem is and how to restructure it. Check that the learner proposes a structure organised around a position (for example, the strongest case, the main objection and a response, leading to a judgement of extent).

topics.name: Thesis statements
topics.description: Write a thesis statement that answers the question with a specific, arguable position, scoped to what the essay can support within its length and evidence, and that may preview the main lines of reasoning. A thesis states what the essay will argue, not merely what it will discuss, and is revised as the argument develops.
masteryEvidence: Writes a thesis that takes a position on the question rather than announcing a topic
Scopes the thesis with qualification and limiting conditions so that it can be supported within the word limit
Distinguishes arguable claims from statements of fact and from unsupported personal preference
Revises the thesis after drafting so that it matches what the essay actually argues
Uses a thesis form suited to the question type (evaluative, causal, comparative)
topics.assessmentPrompt: Give four candidate theses for the same question: a fact, an announcement (‘This essay will discuss…’), an overbroad claim and a qualified, arguable claim. Ask the learner to rank them and improve the weakest. Check that the ranking rewards arguability and feasible scope rather than length or vocabulary.

topics.name: Writing introductions
topics.description: Write an introduction that establishes the context and relevance of the topic, narrows to the specific focus and any key definitions, states the thesis and, where appropriate, outlines the structure, moving efficiently from general to specific. The introduction sets the reader's expectations for the whole essay and is usually best finalised after the body is drafted.
masteryEvidence: Writes an introduction that moves from context to focus to thesis in proportion to the essay's length
Opens with a specific, relevant context rather than a sweeping generalisation or dictionary definition
Defines or delimits key terms where the question requires it
Includes a brief roadmap where length and discipline make one useful, and ensures the body follows it
Revises the introduction after drafting so that it matches the body
topics.assessmentPrompt: Give an introduction that opens with a sweeping claim (‘Since the beginning of history…’), spends most of its length on background and ends without a thesis. Ask the learner to rewrite it in under 150 words. Check for a specific opening, efficient narrowing, a clear thesis and, optionally, a roadmap consistent with the plan.

topics.name: Writing conclusions
topics.description: Write a conclusion that synthesises the argument rather than repeating it, gives a direct answer to the question, and indicates implications, limitations or questions for further work without introducing new evidence. The conclusion is where the essay's overall judgement is made fully explicit and calibrated to the evidence presented.
masteryEvidence: States a direct answer to the question that is consistent with the thesis and the body
Synthesises how the main points together support the answer rather than listing them in order
Identifies a limitation, implication or open question in proportion to the essay
Avoids introducing evidence or claims that were not developed in the body
Calibrates the strength of the final claim to the evidence presented
topics.assessmentPrompt: Give an essay body and a conclusion that lists each paragraph's point and ends with a new claim. Ask the learner to rewrite the conclusion. Check for synthesis rather than summary, a direct answer, appropriately calibrated claims and no new evidence.

topics.name: Organising the essay body
topics.description: Sequence and group body paragraphs so that they build the argument logically—by importance, causal chain, comparison criteria, or concession and rebuttal—and organise source material thematically around the writer's points rather than source by source. The organisation should be visible to the reader through topic sentences and transitions.
masteryEvidence: Chooses and justifies an ordering principle for the body that suits the question
Groups source material by theme or point rather than by author
Places counter-arguments where they can be answered effectively
Signals the organisation through topic sentences and transitions between sections
Reorganises a source-by-source draft into a thematic one
topics.assessmentPrompt: Give a body outline organised by source (paragraph 1 on one author, paragraph 2 on another, and so on). Ask the learner to reorganise it thematically. Check for themes stated as claims, sources distributed across themes, and an order the learner can justify in relation to the thesis.

topics.name: Answering the question
topics.description: Keep every part of an essay relevant to the question as set—its command words, focus and limits—by checking the thesis, topic sentences and conclusion against the question and cutting or reframing material that does not contribute to the answer. Irrelevance and partial answers are among the reasons markers most often give for low marks.
masteryEvidence: Checks each topic sentence against the question and explains how the paragraph contributes to the answer
Identifies material that is accurate but irrelevant and removes or reframes it
Addresses all parts of a multi-part question in proportion to their weight
Makes the link to the question explicit at key points without mechanically repeating the question's wording
topics.assessmentPrompt: Give a question and a draft in which one body paragraph is on the general topic but does not address the question. Ask the learner to identify it and decide whether to cut or reframe it. Check that the reasoning refers to the question's command word and limits, not just to its topic.

topics.name: Essay types
topics.description: Recognise the main types of essay set at university—argumentative (exposition), discussion, explanation and cause–effect, compare–contrast, problem–solution, and commentary or challenge essays—and how their purposes shape the thesis, organisation and conclusion. Types often blend, and labels vary across disciplines, courses and textbooks.
masteryEvidence: Identifies the essay type implied by a question and explains how it shapes the thesis and structure
Distinguishes discussion essays (weighing perspectives towards a judgement) from argumentative essays (defending a position from the outset)
Plans two essays of different types on the same topic
Recognises when a question combines types, for example explaining and then evaluating
topics.assessmentPrompt: Give four questions on one topic with different command words and focuses. Ask the learner to identify the essay type each implies and sketch its structure. Check that they connect type to purpose and organisation rather than mapping command words mechanically to templates.

topics.name: Headings and sections
topics.description: Judge whether headings are expected, permitted or discouraged in a given essay (practice varies by discipline, length and department) and, where they are used, write informative headings in a consistent hierarchy without letting them replace topic sentences and transitions. Reports and dissertations use headings conventionally; many essay traditions do not.
masteryEvidence: States the local convention on headings for a given assignment and follows it
Writes informative headings that indicate the content or claim of a section rather than generic labels
Maintains a consistent heading hierarchy
Keeps topic sentences and transitions so that the text reads coherently with the headings removed
topics.assessmentPrompt: Give a 3,000-word essay draft with generic headings (‘Introduction’, ‘Main body’, ‘Point 1’) and no transitions. Ask whether headings are appropriate and how to improve the draft. Check for informative headings or a justified decision to remove them, and for attention to transitions either way.

topics.name: Depth versus breadth
topics.description: Narrow the scope of an essay to a manageable number of points, cases or perspectives so that each can be analysed in depth, and justify the focus explicitly. Covering everything relevant at a superficial level is a common cause of ‘descriptive’ feedback; within a word limit, depth of analysis is usually valued over breadth of coverage.
masteryEvidence: Narrows a broad question to a defensible focus and states the focus and its rationale in the introduction
Reduces a plan with many points to fewer, better-developed ones
Develops a single point through several layers (explanation, evidence, evaluation, implication)
Acknowledges what has been excluded and why
topics.assessmentPrompt: Give a 1,500-word essay plan with eight points. Ask the learner to cut it to three or four and justify the choice. Check whether they keep the points that matter most for the thesis, merge related ones and plan deeper development rather than simply deleting the last few.

topics.name: Demonstrating criticality in essays
topics.description: Move beyond describing content to analysing how and why, evaluating the strength of evidence and arguments, comparing perspectives and reaching reasoned judgements, and make these moves visible in the text through evaluative language, concession and explicit reasoning. Criticality is among the qualities markers mention most often, and it is understood somewhat differently across disciplines.
masteryEvidence: Distinguishes descriptive, analytical and evaluative sentences in a model essay and in their own writing
Evaluates a source's evidence or method and states the consequence for the essay's argument
Compares perspectives and explains why one is more persuasive in a given context
Uses concession and counter-argument to reach a qualified judgement
Revises a descriptive paragraph so that it includes analysis and evaluation
topics.assessmentPrompt: Give a paragraph that accurately summarises two studies. Ask the learner to add three sentences that make it critical. Check for evaluation of evidence or method, comparison, and a judgement linked to the essay's argument—not merely negative comments.

topics.name: Writing titles
topics.description: Write informative titles for self-chosen essays, reports, dissertations and articles that indicate the topic, focus and, where appropriate, the argument or method, using conventions such as two-part colon titles, and apply the capitalisation rules of the required style. A title is often the first thing a marker, examiner or database user sees.
masteryEvidence: Writes a title that identifies topic, focus and, where appropriate, position or method
Uses a two-part colon title where it helps combine an engaging element with a descriptive one
Applies the required capitalisation style (sentence or title case) consistently
Revises a vague or overlong title to be specific and concise
topics.assessmentPrompt: Give three titles for the same essay: a vague one-word title, an overlong descriptive title and an informative colon title. Ask the learner to rank them and write a better alternative. Check for specificity, concision and consistent capitalisation.

topics.name: The academic paragraph
topics.description: Understand the academic paragraph as a unit that typically develops one controlling idea, signalled to the reader and developed through explanation and evidence, and that serves the purpose of the whole text. The one-idea paragraph is a reliable default for planning and reading, although expert writers vary paragraph structure according to function and discipline.
masteryEvidence: Identifies the controlling idea of a paragraph and the sentences that develop it
Explains why a paragraph that combines two unrelated points is harder for a reader to follow
Divides a multi-point paragraph into coherent paragraphs at changes of controlling idea
Recognises an effective paragraph whose main point is placed late or left implicit, and explains the effect
topics.assessmentPrompt: Give a 150-word paragraph that contains two separate points. Ask the learner where they would divide it and why. Check that the division follows a change of controlling idea rather than length or the position of a linking word.

topics.name: Writing topic sentences
topics.description: Write sentences that state a paragraph's controlling idea precisely enough to predict and constrain what follows, and that connect the paragraph to the thesis or the previous paragraph. Effective topic sentences make claims rather than announce topics, and read in sequence they give the reader an outline of the argument.
masteryEvidence: Writes topic sentences that make a claim the paragraph then supports, rather than naming a topic or stating a fact
Pitches the controlling idea at a level of generality that one paragraph can support
Links topic sentences to the thesis or previous paragraph through reference, signalling nouns or explicit connection
Revises either the topic sentence or the paragraph body so that the two match
Places the main point after a brief transitional or contextual opener when the paragraph needs one
topics.assessmentPrompt: Give three candidate opening sentences for the same paragraph: a fact, a topic announcement and a claim. Ask which works best and why. Then supply a paragraph body without its first sentence and ask for a topic sentence. Check that it is a claim the body actually supports and is neither broader nor narrower than the content.

topics.name: Developing support
topics.description: Develop a controlling idea with a suitable combination of explanation, reasoning, evidence, examples and analysis, choosing support that is relevant and sufficient for the strength of the claim and stating how it supports the claim. Paragraphs that assert without support, or pile up examples without explanation, are a frequent cause of ‘underdeveloped’ or ‘descriptive’ feedback.
masteryEvidence: Supports a claim with at least two different kinds of development (explanation, data, example, comparison, concession)
Selects evidence that bears directly on the controlling idea and is appropriate to the claim's strength
Writes sentences that explain how evidence supports the claim rather than leaving the link implicit
Distinguishes illustration (an example) from evidence (data or research findings) and uses each appropriately
Identifies under-supported claims in a draft and adds development
topics.assessmentPrompt: Give a paragraph with a clear topic sentence followed only by two examples. Ask the learner what is missing and to add two sentences. Look for explanation of how the examples support the claim, or a qualification of the claim, rather than a third example.

topics.name: Point–evidence–explanation–link structures
topics.description: Use PEEL-type scaffolds (point, evidence, explanation, link, and variants such as PEE or PEEL-C) to construct supported paragraphs while learning, and recognise their limits: many paragraphs need several pieces of evidence, a counter-point or no explicit link, and mechanical application produces formulaic text. The aim is to internalise the functions the scaffold names and then write without it.
masteryEvidence: Writes a paragraph that realises each PEEL function without needing labels
Maps the PEEL functions onto an authentic academic paragraph and notes where it departs from the pattern
Adapts the pattern for paragraphs with several sources, a counter-argument or a transitional purpose
Recognises when a formulaic link sentence adds nothing and omits it
topics.assessmentPrompt: Give a published academic paragraph and ask the learner to label it using PEEL. Check whether they can map the functions and also notice what the paragraph does that PEEL does not describe, such as several pieces of evidence, a concession or the absence of a final link.

topics.name: Internal paragraph coherence
topics.description: Order and connect the sentences of a paragraph so that each follows logically from the previous one and from the controlling idea, using given-before-new information structure, thematic progression, consistent reference and lexical chains, with explicit connectors where a logical relation needs signalling. Coherence depends on logic and information flow far more than on the number of linking words.
masteryEvidence: Begins sentences with information already introduced and places new information towards the end
Maintains unambiguous reference chains (repeated terms, pronouns, this + noun) through a paragraph
Uses connectors only where they state a relation the reader needs, and chooses them precisely
Locates a break in coherence in a peer's paragraph and explains its cause
Explains why adding linking words does not repair a paragraph whose sentences are poorly ordered
topics.assessmentPrompt: Give a grammatically accurate paragraph in which one sentence introduces a new topic in subject position without any link to what precedes it. Ask the learner to find where the reader loses the thread and fix it. Check whether they reorder or rephrase the sentence opening rather than insert ‘Moreover’ or ‘Furthermore’.

topics.name: Concluding and linking sentences
topics.description: Close a paragraph, where useful, with a sentence that draws out the significance of its content for the argument, qualifies it, or prepares the next point, rather than repeating the topic sentence. Not every paragraph needs a separate concluding sentence; the choice depends on the paragraph's length and function.
masteryEvidence: Writes a closing sentence that states what the paragraph's evidence shows for the thesis
Distinguishes a closing sentence that adds significance from one that restates the topic sentence
Writes a forward-linking sentence where the next paragraph builds on the current one
Omits a separate closing sentence where the final point already closes the paragraph, and can explain why
topics.assessmentPrompt: Give a paragraph that ends by restating its topic sentence. Ask the learner to replace the final sentence with one that says what the paragraph shows. Check that the new sentence goes beyond restatement, for example by drawing an implication, qualifying the claim or linking it to the question.

topics.name: Paragraph length and division
topics.description: Decide where to begin a new paragraph according to shifts in point, function or stage of the argument, and keep paragraphs long enough to develop an idea but short enough not to overload the reader, generally avoiding one-sentence paragraphs and page-long blocks in essays. Conventions vary with genre, discipline and medium.
masteryEvidence: Divides an overlong paragraph at a shift in point or function
Develops or merges single-sentence paragraphs that lack support
Explains when a short paragraph is effective, for example as a transition or for emphasis
Adjusts paragraph length to genre and medium (essay, report, blog post, email)
topics.assessmentPrompt: Give a 450-word single paragraph and a sequence of four one-sentence paragraphs on related points. Ask the learner to repair both. Check that divisions follow shifts in point and that the short paragraphs are developed or merged rather than simply joined.

topics.name: Paragraph functions
topics.description: Recognise and write paragraphs that serve different functions within a text—introductory, body (argument, evidence, counter-argument), transitional and concluding—and understand that each function calls for different internal organisation and language. Treating every paragraph as a body paragraph produces weak introductions, conclusions and transitions.
masteryEvidence: Identifies the function of each paragraph in a model text
Describes how introductory and concluding paragraphs differ in organisation from body paragraphs
Writes a short transitional paragraph that summarises one section and previews the next
Writes a counter-argument paragraph that presents and then responds to an opposing view
topics.assessmentPrompt: Give the paragraphs of a short essay in random order. Ask the learner to identify each paragraph's function and reconstruct the order. Check that function, not only content, guides their decisions—for example that they place the counter-argument paragraph where it can be answered.

topics.name: Integrating sources in paragraphs
topics.description: Integrate source material into a paragraph so that the writer's point leads, sources are introduced and attributed, and each piece of evidence is followed by commentary that interprets, evaluates or connects it (introduce–cite–comment). This keeps the writer's voice in control and distinguishes argument from a chain of summaries.
masteryEvidence: Opens source-based paragraphs with their own claim rather than with a source
Introduces evidence with a signal phrase or citation form suited to its role in the paragraph
Follows each piece of source evidence with commentary that explains its relevance or evaluates it
Marks clearly where attributed content ends and their own comment begins
Uses more than one source in a paragraph and states the relationship between them
topics.assessmentPrompt: Give a paragraph consisting of three consecutive source summaries. Ask the learner to rewrite it so that their own point leads. Check for a writer's claim, selective use of the sources, commentary after the evidence and clear attribution boundaries.

topics.name: Writing as a recursive process
topics.description: Understand academic writing as interleaved planning, translating (putting ideas into language) and reviewing, revisited recursively rather than performed once in sequence, and distinguish knowledge-telling (writing down what one knows in the order it is recalled) from knowledge-transforming (reworking content to meet rhetorical goals). The model explains why much of the thinking in academic writing happens during drafting and revision, and why early surface correction can be counter-productive.
masteryEvidence: Describes their own composing process for a recent assignment and identifies where planning, drafting and reviewing overlapped or looped back
Distinguishes, in two sample texts on the same question, writing that reproduces recalled content from writing that reorganises content to answer the question
Sets a rhetorical goal before drafting (what the reader should accept by the end) and checks the draft against it
Explains why fixing surface errors early can interrupt idea development, and schedules editing accordingly
topics.assessmentPrompt: Ask the learner to talk through how they produced their last 500-word assignment, step by step. Listen for whether they describe a single linear pass (read, write, check spelling) or loops back to planning after drafting, and whether they mention changing ideas, not only words, while writing.

topics.name: Analysing assignment and exam tasks
topics.description: Unpack an assignment brief or question to identify the command word(s), the topic and its limits, required sources, genre and reader, word limit and marking criteria, and turn these into a working statement of what the text must do. Task representation shapes every later writing decision, and misreading the task is a common, avoidable cause of low marks.
masteryEvidence: Rewrites an assignment question in their own words, separating the instruction, the topic and any limiting conditions (period, context, theory)
Identifies what each command word in a multi-part question requires and how the parts relate
Lists the explicit requirements of a brief (genre, length, sources, format, deadline) and flags any that are ambiguous
Links at least two marking criteria to concrete decisions about content or structure
Formulates an appropriate clarification question to a tutor when a brief is genuinely ambiguous
topics.assessmentPrompt: Give a multi-part question that asks learners to outline a policy and evaluate its effectiveness in a named context. Ask the learner what a full answer must contain. Check whether they notice both command words, the limiting context and the implied need for a judgement, rather than only the topic.

topics.name: Generating ideas
topics.description: Use deliberate techniques—brainstorming, focused freewriting, question heuristics, mapping and talking ideas through—to produce more and better content than first recall provides, and then select from it in the light of the task. Separating generation from evaluation helps writers get beyond the first, most obvious points.
masteryEvidence: Produces a range of candidate points for a question using at least two different techniques
Extends an initial idea with question heuristics (why, how, under what conditions, according to whom, so what)
Selects and discards generated ideas with explicit reference to the task, explaining the choices
Turns points that need support into reading or search questions
topics.assessmentPrompt: Give a question and five minutes to generate ideas by any method, then two minutes to choose the three most useful. Check the quantity and range of ideas, whether any go beyond the obvious, and whether the selection is justified by the question rather than by ease of writing.

topics.name: Planning and outlining
topics.description: Turn a position and selected evidence into a hierarchical plan that sequences points, attaches support to each and shows how each part advances the answer, in a format (linear outline, map, table) suited to the writer and task. A plan is a working hypothesis to be revised during drafting, not a contract.
masteryEvidence: Produces an outline in which each main entry is a claim linked to the overall position, not a topic label
Attaches specific evidence or sources to each point and marks gaps
Orders points according to a stated rationale (importance, causal logic, chronology, concession then rebuttal)
Estimates a word allocation for each section of the plan
Revises the outline when drafting shows a point is weak or misplaced, and explains the change
topics.assessmentPrompt: Ask for an outline for a 1,500-word essay on a familiar question. Check whether entries are claims or merely topics (‘Economic factors’ versus ‘Economic factors outweigh political ones because…’), whether evidence is attached to each, and whether the order is justified.

topics.name: Drafting
topics.description: Produce a complete first draft from a plan, keeping momentum by deferring sentence-level correction, marking gaps to fill later and allowing the argument to develop as it is written. Treating the first draft as provisional makes revision possible and reduces the paralysis of trying to write a final version first time.
masteryEvidence: Completes a full draft of a set length within an agreed time without stopping to polish individual sentences
Uses placeholders for missing references, words or data and resolves them in a later session
Notes where drafting changed or sharpened the planned argument and updates the plan
Distinguishes a draft from a finished text when deciding what feedback to request
topics.assessmentPrompt: Set 25 minutes to draft 400 words from a supplied plan. Afterwards ask: did you stop to correct, how many placeholders did you use, and did you finish? A complete, imperfect draft with marked gaps is the target; a polished but unfinished one indicates the gap.

topics.name: Integrating reading into writing
topics.description: Move from reading and notes to one's own text by selecting source content for its relevance to the task, organising it around one's own points rather than the sources' order, and connecting it with commentary. This discourse-synthesis process underlies most university writing, which is source-based rather than written from personal knowledge.
masteryEvidence: Selects from notes only the source content that serves the current point, leaving out accurate but irrelevant material
Reorganises source content under their own points rather than following the order of the sources
Drafts from notes with the source closed, reducing reliance on source wording
Adds their own interpretation or connection after source content
Keeps track of which idea came from which source throughout drafting
topics.assessmentPrompt: Give two short texts and a question, allow 15 minutes for reading and note-making, then remove the texts and ask for one paragraph written from the notes. Check selection (relevant content only), organisation (around the learner's point), attribution and the presence of the learner's own commentary.

topics.name: Audience and purpose
topics.description: Recognise that most assessed university writing addresses an expert reader who knows the content but expects the writer to display understanding, make reasoning explicit and argue a position, and adjust content, explicitness and register to that reader and to the text's purpose. Mismatched assumptions about the reader explain many ‘too descriptive’ or ‘explain this’ comments.
masteryEvidence: Identifies the reader and purpose of a given assignment and explains how they differ from those of a blog post or exam answer on the same topic
Explains why defining key terms and stating reasoning is expected even though the marker already knows the content
Adjusts the amount of background explanation in a draft to the stated readership
Distinguishes demonstrating understanding through argument from reporting information
topics.assessmentPrompt: Show a paragraph that explains basic background at length and then asserts a conclusion without reasons. Ask what a marker would think and what the writer should change. Look for recognition that the marker needs reasoning and a position made explicit, not more background.

topics.name: Managing extended writing projects
topics.description: Plan and sustain projects of several thousand words or more by breaking them into dated milestones, budgeting words and time across sections, writing regularly rather than in a final burst, scheduling feedback, and tracking versions and progress. Extended projects such as pre-sessional research projects, dissertations and theses often falter through poor management rather than weak language.
masteryEvidence: Produces a backward-planned schedule from the deadline with dated milestones for reading, drafting, feedback and editing
Allocates a word budget across sections and monitors it during drafting
Maintains a regular writing routine and records output across several weeks
Revises the schedule after slippage while protecting time for revision
Times feedback requests so that there is time to act on the feedback
topics.assessmentPrompt: Ask the learner to produce a one-page plan for a 5,000-word project due in eight weeks alongside other commitments. Check for backward planning, a word budget, time reserved for feedback and revision, and realistic weekly targets.

topics.name: Overcoming writing blocks
topics.description: Recognise likely causes of being unable to start or continue writing—perfectionism, rigid rules, an unclear task, anxiety about language or evaluation, fatigue—and apply matched strategies such as freewriting, generative writing, lowering the stakes of drafts, starting with an easier section or breaking the task down. Blocks are common at every level, including among experienced researchers, and are usually solvable.
masteryEvidence: Identifies the probable cause of a recent block (unclear task, rigid rule, fear of judgement, fatigue)
Applies a strategy matched to the cause, such as freewriting, starting with a methods or body section, or a short timed goal
Replaces an absolute rule (for example ‘the introduction must be written first’) with a flexible heuristic
Seeks appropriate support (writing group, tutor, writing centre) when a block persists
topics.assessmentPrompt: Present three short scenarios of blocked writers: a perfectionist, one with an unclear task and one anxious about their English. Ask the learner to diagnose each and suggest a first step. Check whether strategies are matched to causes rather than generic (‘work harder’, ‘read more’).

topics.name: Using the first language in composing
topics.description: Use the first language and other languages strategically while composing in English—for generating ideas, planning, note-making, checking meaning and solving lexical problems—while drafting the text predominantly in English and using machine translation transparently and within local rules. Plurilingual composing is a resource. Evidence on drafting fully in another language and then translating is mixed: it can support content and organisation, especially at lower proficiency, but may carry over source-language structures, reduce L2 practice and, with machine translation, breach assessment rules.
masteryEvidence: Describes which composing activities they carry out in which language and why
Uses L1 or mixed-language notes and plans to support an English draft without translating sentence by sentence
Checks terms and collocations derived from the L1 against English sources, dictionaries or corpora
States the module's or institution's rules on machine translation and complies with them
topics.assessmentPrompt: Ask the learner to show the notes and plan for a recent assignment and explain which languages they used at each stage. Check whether other languages support thinking and planning, and whether the English text was drafted from these rather than translated in full.

topics.name: Working within word limits
topics.description: Plan to a word limit by allocating words across sections in proportion to their importance, cut over-length drafts by removing low-value content before trimming sentences, expand under-length drafts by developing analysis rather than adding background, and follow local conventions on what counts (references, headings, tables, appendices) and on tolerances. Meeting a limit is a matter of prioritisation, not only concision.
masteryEvidence: Produces a word budget that gives most words to the sections that carry the argument
Cuts an over-length draft by removing or compressing whole points, background or repetition before editing sentences
States what the module includes in the word count and any tolerance or penalty, citing the source of the rule
Expands an under-length draft by developing analysis rather than adding description
topics.assessmentPrompt: Give a 600-word draft that must be cut to 450 words. Check whether the learner first removes or compresses low-value content (background, repetition, surplus examples) and preserves the argument, rather than trimming every sentence evenly or cutting the analysis.

topics.name: Formatting and presentation
topics.description: Present a text according to the required conventions—style guide, departmental template, cover sheet, page layout, heading levels, numbering of figures and tables, font and spacing—and apply them consistently using word-processing styles. Presentation rarely carries much weight in marking, but it affects readability, the reader's first impression and sometimes compliance with submission rules.
masteryEvidence: Locates and follows the formatting requirements in an assignment brief, handbook or style guide
Applies consistent heading levels, page numbering, spacing and figure and table numbering
Uses built-in styles and automatic numbering rather than manual formatting
Checks the final document against a formatting checklist before submission
topics.assessmentPrompt: Give a two-page document with six formatting inconsistencies and a one-page style sheet. Ask the learner to find and fix them. Check accuracy and whether they use styles rather than manual changes that will break when the text is edited.

dependencies.reason: Distinguishing revision from editing presupposes understanding reviewing as a recursive sub-process that can change content, not only correct form
Learners must distinguish whole-text revision from sentence-level editing before they can prioritise it
Global revision rereads the draft from the intended reader's perspective
Reverse outlining requires stating each paragraph's controlling idea as a claim, the skill practised in writing topic sentences
Reverse outlining is a technique for diagnosing the whole-text problems that global revision addresses
Style editing is the sentence-level stage, distinguished from and normally following revision
Editing for concision applies techniques for removing redundancy and wordiness
Editing for clarity applies principles such as keeping subject and verb close and placing heavy elements late
Editing for register requires knowing which features mark formal academic style, as tendencies rather than absolute rules
Grammar editing is a distinct stage that should follow revision
Targeted editing depends on having identified one's own persistent error patterns
Run-ons, comma splices and fragments are among the most frequent targets of grammar editing
Proofreading is defined as the final, surface-level stage and must be distinguished from revision and editing
Checking spelling consistency requires knowing the conventions of British and American spelling and commonly confused words
Apostrophes, hyphens and dashes are frequent sources of surface error checked at proofreading
Self-assessment against criteria presupposes being able to interpret rubrics and grade descriptors
Turning a self-assessment into a revision plan requires knowing which level of change each criterion calls for
Reviewers need to know what global problems look like in order to prioritise them in feedback
Criteria-referenced peer feedback applies the same evaluative judgement used in self-assessment
Receiving and using peer comments draws on appreciating feedback, managing affect and taking action
Phrasing critical comments to peers requires awareness of face and mitigation
Evaluating a tool's grammar suggestions requires enough grammatical knowledge and checking routine to accept or reject them
Spell-checkers supplement but do not replace proofreading, for example of correctly spelt wrong words
Judging AI rewriting suggestions depends on understanding that such tools generate plausible text that may change meaning
Proofreading policies are defined by the difference between surface correction and changes to content, argument and structure
Unpermitted third-party editing is a form of unauthorised collaboration, so the boundary between collaboration and collusion must be understood
Essays are built from paragraphs that each develop one point, so the paragraph unit is usually taught first
Essay structure is organised around a central argument, which requires understanding argument as a reasoned position rather than a list of facts
The thesis is the controlling claim that the whole structure is built to support
Writing an arguable thesis requires distinguishing claims of fact, cause, value and policy
Scoping a thesis to what can be supported uses the language of bounded generalisation and qualification
An introduction moves the reader towards the thesis, so the thesis must exist first
Introductory paragraphs have a distinct function and internal organisation from body paragraphs
Roadmaps and statements of scope use frame markers and advance organisers
A conclusion answers the question by restating and developing the thesis in the light of the body
Concluding paragraphs have a distinct synthesising function
Conclusions draw on the language of summarising and concluding
Stating a final judgement, implications and limits requires matching claim strength to the evidence presented
The body is ordered to build the case for the thesis, which supplies the organising logic
Organisation is made visible to the reader through topic sentences that state each paragraph's contribution
Patterns such as problem–solution and claim–counterclaim provide principled orders for body sections
Thematic rather than source-by-source organisation depends on understanding synthesis
Relevance can only be judged against an accurate representation of what the question asks
Relevance is maintained by checking each part of the essay against a thesis that answers the question
Topic sentences are the main place where each paragraph's link to the question is made explicit
Essay types are variations on the basic thesis-led structure, so the general structure must be understood first
Recognising the essay type a question implies relies partly on interpreting its command words
Essay types are realised through characteristic text patterns such as cause–effect and problem–solution
Headings label sections of an organisation that must already be logically sequenced
Heading levels and their visual hierarchy follow the formatting conventions of the required style
Points are selected for depth according to how well they serve the thesis
Narrowing an essay's scope applies the same procedure as focusing a broad topic into a manageable question
Choosing between depth and breadth is driven by the word budget available
Demonstrating criticality in writing requires first distinguishing description from analysis and evaluation
Critical evaluation in an essay serves a position; without a thesis, evaluation becomes free-floating comment
Evaluating evidence in one's essay draws on judging the relevance, sufficiency and quality of evidence in reading
Making critique visible and appropriately mitigated requires the language of evaluating others' work
An informative title is derived from the essay's focus and, often, its thesis
Titles follow sentence-case or title-case conventions of the required style
Recognising a main idea and its supporting detail in reading is the receptive basis for writing paragraphs organised around one controlling idea
A topic sentence states the controlling idea, so the learner must first understand the paragraph as a one-idea unit
Support is selected and judged for relevance against the claim stated in the topic sentence
Illustrating a claim draws on the language of exemplification and choosing representative examples
Explaining how evidence supports a claim uses the language of reasons, mechanisms and justification
Choosing sufficient and appropriate support requires distinguishing anecdotal, statistical, expert and empirical evidence
PEEL packages the functions of developing support (evidence and explanation) into a scaffold
The link move in PEEL is a form of paragraph closure
Internal coherence is judged against the controlling idea set up by the topic sentence
Ordering information within and across sentences applies the given–new principle
A concluding sentence develops or draws out the significance of the controlling idea stated at the start
Closing sentences use the language of summarising and drawing conclusions
Deciding where to break depends on recognising where one controlling idea ends and another begins
Introductory, transitional and concluding functions are defined by a paragraph's place in the overall structure of the text
Source evidence is one form of paragraph support and must serve the paragraph's claim
Introducing and attributing evidence, and marking where attributed content ends, uses signal phrases
Most integrated evidence is paraphrased rather than quoted
Keeping the writer's voice in control depends on distinguishing claims the writer makes from claims attributed to sources
Representing what a question requires depends on knowing what command words such as evaluate, discuss and to what extent demand
A full task representation includes the reader and purpose the text is written for, beyond the question wording
Treating generation as a separate, revisitable sub-process of planning presupposes a recursive model of composing
Ideas are generated for, and later selected against, the writer's representation of the task
Outlining selects from and organises material that has already been generated
Claim-based outlines require understanding an argument as a position supported by reasons and evidence rather than a list of topics
Linear outlines, maps and tables used for planning are the formats first learned for note-making
Drafting usually proceeds from a plan that supplies sequence and content, which frees attention for formulation
Drafts are composed paragraph by paragraph, each developing one controlling idea
Writing from notes rather than the open source depends on notes that record source details and separate source content from the writer's own comment
Transforming selected source content into the writer's text relies on paraphrase
Condensing source passages to their main idea is the usual first step in using them as evidence
Selecting and organising reading around the assignment question precedes integrating that reading into a draft
Adjusting writing to reader and purpose builds on the understanding that language varies with tenor, field and mode
Scheduling milestones for an extended text applies general planning, prioritising and time-protection strategies
Monitoring progress on a long text uses word budgets allocated across sections
Most strategies for blocks depend on accepting drafts as provisional and deferring correction
Diagnosing a block and choosing a strategy is an instance of monitoring and adjusting one's own performance
Other languages are most productively used during generating and planning, so learners need to recognise these sub-processes
Strategic L1 use in composing applies a broader view of the plurilingual repertoire as a learning resource
Word budgets are allocated across the sections of a plan
Once structural cuts are made, sentence-level trimming uses concision techniques
Formatting requirements are part of the brief and must be identified before they can be applied
Consistent formatting is applied most reliably through word-processing styles and automatic numbering
Evidence integrated in a paragraph must carry an in-text citation placed correctly relative to the signal phrase or the borrowed content

guidance.summary: Sommers (1980) found that student writers mostly revised at word level, whereas experienced writers revised argument and structure; Zamel (1983) reported similar contrasts among ESL writers. In Flower and Hayes's (1981) model, reviewing includes both evaluating and revising and can occur at any point in composing. Teach the three levels explicitly and ask learners to sequence them, because many equate ‘checking’ with grammar correction.

activities.title: Change classification
learnerActions: Compare two drafts of the same text
Classify every change as revision, editing or proofreading
Discuss which changes improved the text most
activities.intendedInsight: The changes that matter most are usually global.
activities.rationale: Draws directly on Sommers's (1980) contrast between student and experienced writers' revisions.

activities.title: Three-pass plan
learnerActions: Plan three passes through your own draft, each with a different focus
Carry out the global pass first and record what changed
activities.intendedInsight: Sequencing saves time and improves quality.
activities.rationale: Separates the reviewing sub-processes described by Flower and Hayes (1981) into manageable tasks.

difficulties.pattern: ‘Revising means correcting the grammar.’
difficulties.revealedBy: Second drafts identical in structure to the first, with surface corrections only.
difficulties.response: Require at least one documented global change per redraft.

difficulties.pattern: Editing sentences that are later cut.
difficulties.revealedBy: Time spent on polished but irrelevant paragraphs.
difficulties.response: Use the three-pass plan and postpone sentence work until structure is settled.

diagnostic.task: Ask the learner how they would use two hours to improve a complete first draft due tomorrow.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Allocates time first to argument and structure, then sentences, then surface checks, with reasons.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Mentions content and structure but plans to start with grammar.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Plans only grammar, spelling and formatting checks.

guidance.contextNotes: At foundation level, use the distinction to structure multi-draft tasks. Pre-sessional and in-sessional learners apply it to their own assignments and feedback requests. The distinction is also the basis of institutional proofreading policies (see edt.proofreading-ethics).
reviewNotes: Sommers (1980) studied L1 writers; its application to L2 writers is supported in broad terms by Zamel (1983).

guidance.summary: Experienced writers revise for argument and with a reader in mind (Sommers, 1980), and the skilled ESL writers in Zamel's (1983) study behaved similarly. Hyland (2003) discusses the place of teacher and peer feedback on content in multi-draft writing classrooms. Teach global revision through structured prompts (thesis check, reverse outline, reader questions), require evidence of structural change between drafts, and give feedback on content before feedback on language.

activities.title: Thesis–body check
learnerActions: Write the thesis and the point of each paragraph on one sheet
Mark where paragraphs do not support the thesis
Decide whether to revise the thesis or the body
activities.intendedInsight: Many drafts argue something different from their stated thesis.
activities.rationale: Targets the gap between intention and text that Sommers (1980) associated with experienced writers' revision.

activities.title: Reader-questions round
learnerActions: A peer reads the draft and notes three places where they could not follow or were not convinced
The writer plans one structural change in response and explains it
activities.intendedInsight: Readers reveal problems that writers cannot see in their own texts.
activities.rationale: Reader response on content is central to multi-draft process teaching (Hyland, 2003).

difficulties.pattern: Reluctance to cut or restructure text that took effort to write.
difficulties.revealedBy: Drafts that only grow; deleted material reinserted later.
difficulties.response: Keep a ‘cuttings’ file so that nothing feels lost, and show examples of productive large cuts.

difficulties.pattern: Unable to see global problems in one's own text.
difficulties.revealedBy: Self-review notes that list only grammar and vocabulary.
difficulties.response: Provide structured prompts, reverse outlining and peer reading. Do not rely on ‘read it again carefully’.

diagnostic.task: Give a draft with a thesis–body mismatch and a missing counter-argument and ask for a revision plan in bullet points.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Identifies both global problems, prioritises them and proposes specific structural changes.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Identifies one global problem but mixes the plan with sentence-level edits.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Lists language corrections only.

guidance.contextNotes: Foundation learners need highly structured revision prompts. Pre-sessional programmes with portfolio assessment can require revision commentaries. PGT writers often revise under severe time pressure and need efficient diagnostic routines. Doctoral writers revise chapters across many drafts in dialogue with supervisors.

guidance.summary: Reverse outlining applies summarisation to one's own text: reducing each paragraph to its gist uses the deletion, generalisation and construction rules described by Brown and Day (1983). It supports the whole-text revision that Sommers (1980) associated with experienced writers. Introduce the technique on a supplied draft with known problems, then transfer it to learners' own drafts; it scales well to dissertations and theses.

activities.title: Outline someone else's draft
learnerActions: Reverse-outline a supplied draft that has known structural problems
Compare outlines in pairs
Agree on the three most important revisions
activities.intendedInsight: Structural problems become visible in outline form that are hard to see in continuous prose.
activities.rationale: Practising on another writer's text reduces the familiarity that hides problems in one's own (Sommers, 1980).

activities.title: Point and function
learnerActions: Write each paragraph's point and its function (claim, evidence, counter-argument, transition)
Read the sequence of functions and look for missing or misplaced moves
activities.intendedInsight: A sequence of functions can reveal a missing counter-argument or a conclusion that arrives too early.
activities.rationale: Summarising to gist relies on the macrorules that Brown and Day (1983) identified in skilled summarising.

difficulties.pattern: Outline entries describe topics (‘about pollution’) rather than points.
difficulties.revealedBy: Outlines made of nouns that reveal nothing about the argument.
difficulties.response: Require each entry to be a full-sentence claim.

difficulties.pattern: Writing the outline from memory of the plan rather than from the draft.
difficulties.revealedBy: An outline that matches the plan but not the actual text.
difficulties.response: Outline one paragraph at a time from the text, with the plan put away.

diagnostic.task: Ask the learner to reverse-outline a five-paragraph draft in ten minutes and name one structural problem.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Accurate point statements; identifies a real structural problem such as a repeated point or misplaced paragraph.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Accurate statements but no problem identified, or a problem identified at sentence level.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Topic labels only, or the outline reproduces the plan.

guidance.contextNotes: Pre-sessional learners can use reverse outlining on extended projects. In-sessional undergraduates and PGT students use it under time pressure before submission. Doctoral researchers can apply it at chapter level, outlining sections as well as paragraphs.
reviewNotes: Reverse outlining is widely recommended in writing-centre practice but has little direct empirical research; the citations support its rationale rather than its tested efficacy.

guidance.summary: Hinkel (2004) provides practical techniques for teaching the vocabulary and grammar of academic style to L2 writers, and Biber and Gray (2010) show that academic writing is compressed mainly through phrasal rather than clausal complexity, which explains both what learners aim for and why over-dense text can be hard to read. Swales and Feak (2012) offer graduate-level guidance on flow and style. Teach style editing as a set of purposeful operations with reasons, and avoid prescriptive myths such as ‘the passive is always more objective’ or ‘never use I’.

activities.title: Edit with reasons
learnerActions: Edit a paragraph
Annotate each edit with its purpose (clarity, concision, register, precision)
Compare edits in pairs and resolve differences
activities.intendedInsight: Good edits have reasons; edits without a reason often make text worse.
activities.rationale: Making the purpose of each change explicit reflects the technique-based approach to academic style in Hinkel (2004).

activities.title: Unpack and repack
learnerActions: Unpack an over-dense noun phrase into clauses
Repack a wordy clausal sentence into phrases
Decide which version suits the intended reader
activities.intendedInsight: Information density is a choice to be calibrated to the reader, not a fixed target.
activities.rationale: Builds on the description of phrasal compression in academic prose (Biber & Gray, 2010).

difficulties.pattern: ‘Academic style means long words and long sentences.’
difficulties.revealedBy: Inflated vocabulary; sentences that readers cannot parse on first reading.
difficulties.response: Show concise expert prose and edit for clarity first.

difficulties.pattern: Applying style myths as absolute rules (‘never use I’, ‘always use the passive’).
difficulties.revealedBy: Awkward passives, dangling modifiers, contorted impersonal constructions.
difficulties.response: Check each rule against exemplars or corpus evidence from the learner's discipline.

diagnostic.task: Give a 100-word paragraph with four style problems and ask for an edited version with brief reasons.
diagnostic.strongResponse: All four problems addressed; meaning preserved; reasons accurate; no new problems introduced.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Two or three problems addressed, or edits that are correct but unexplained.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Synonym substitution with no gain in clarity, or meaning changed.

guidance.contextNotes: Pre-sessional learners focus on register and concision. In-sessional undergraduates and PGT writers need disciplinary style conventions. Doctoral researchers edit for publication, where concision and clarity for specialist readers are judged by reviewers and editors.

guidance.summary: Whether written corrective feedback improves accuracy has been debated (Truscott, 1996; Ferris, 1999). Later work, including Bitchener and Ferris (2012) and Kang and Han's (2015) meta-analysis, suggests that feedback can improve written accuracy, with effects moderated by factors such as proficiency and instructional setting. Ferris has long argued for helping learners become independent self-editors who focus on frequent, rule-governed error patterns. Teach targeted editing passes, use error logs, and pair feedback with opportunities to revise.

activities.title: Error profile
learnerActions: Collect three recently corrected texts
Tally error types
Choose three to target and write a personal editing checklist
activities.intendedInsight: A few recurrent error types account for much of the correction a learner receives.
activities.rationale: Focusing on frequent, rule-governed patterns reflects the selective approach to error treatment discussed by Bitchener and Ferris (2012).

activities.title: One error type, one pass
learnerActions: Edit a draft for one targeted error type only
Record the number of instances found
Repeat with the next error type on the checklist
activities.intendedInsight: Focused passes find more errors than a single general reading.
activities.rationale: Supports the shift from teacher correction to learner self-editing argued for by Ferris (1999).

difficulties.pattern: Reading the whole text once for ‘all errors’ and finding few.
difficulties.revealedBy: Recurrent errors left uncorrected in final versions.
difficulties.response: Replace general rereading with separate targeted passes.

difficulties.pattern: Expecting the teacher to correct every error.
difficulties.revealedBy: Requests for full correction; frustration with coded or selective feedback.
difficulties.response: Explain the rationale for selective feedback and self-editing. Do not provide comprehensive correction on every draft, which shifts responsibility away from the learner.

difficulties.pattern: Article errors persist because the learner's first language has no article system or marks definiteness through other means, such as word order or demonstratives.
difficulties.revealedBy: Omitted or overused articles, especially with generic and abstract nouns.
difficulties.response: Target a small number of high-frequency article contexts with rule-of-thumb checks and accept gradual development; do not expect elimination of article errors within a single course.

diagnostic.task: Give a 200-word paragraph containing eight errors of the learner's known types plus four others, and ask for editing in eight minutes.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Finds most errors of their targeted types and some others, using a systematic approach.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Finds some targeted errors but works unsystematically.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Finds few errors, or introduces new ones.

guidance.contextNotes: Foundation learners need simple checklists and supported practice. Pre-sessional programmes often assess accuracy, so error logs and editing passes fit well into multi-draft cycles. Postgraduate and doctoral writers usually have fewer but more persistent error types and benefit from corpus checking.
reviewNotes: The written corrective feedback debate remains contested in its details; this topic does not take a position on direct versus indirect feedback.

guidance.summary: Writers miss surface errors in their own texts partly because they read for meaning they already know; proofreading techniques work by making the text unfamiliar. There is little dedicated research on proofreading techniques for L2 writers, so present them as practical strategies for learners to trial and evaluate.
