Ferris's work on self-editing (Bitchener & Ferris, 2012) supports teaching learners to monitor their own surface errors rather than relying on correction by others.

activities.title: Technique trial
learnerActions: Proofread one short text silently and another aloud or in a different font and layout
Compare how many planted errors each method found
Choose techniques for the next assignment
activities.intendedInsight: Changing how the text looks or sounds reveals errors that silent rereading misses.
activities.rationale: Learners test techniques on their own performance rather than accepting them on authority.

activities.title: Personal proofreading checklist
learnerActions: Combine common surface errors and personal ones from feedback into a checklist
Use it on a final draft and note which items found errors
activities.intendedInsight: A personal checklist makes proofreading faster and more reliable.
activities.rationale: Connects proofreading to self-monitoring of personal error patterns (Bitchener & Ferris, 2012).

difficulties.pattern: Relying entirely on the spell-checker.
difficulties.revealedBy: Correctly spelt wrong words (form/from, their/there, causal/casual).
difficulties.response: Teach a homophone and near-miss check as part of proofreading.

difficulties.pattern: Proofreading while drafting rather than at the end.
difficulties.revealedBy: Slow drafting combined with errors remaining in the final version.
difficulties.response: Separate stages explicitly and schedule a final proofreading session.

difficulties.pattern: Mixing British and American spelling within one text.
difficulties.revealedBy: Inconsistent -ise/-ize, -our/-or spellings and dictionary settings.
difficulties.response: Set the word processor's language, choose one variety (or follow the required style) and check consistency as a separate pass.

diagnostic.task: Give a 250-word text with ten planted surface errors and five minutes.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Finds eight or more, including homophones and consistency errors, using deliberate techniques.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Finds five to seven, mainly obvious misspellings.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Finds fewer than five or makes new errors.

guidance.contextNotes: Foundation and pre-sessional learners benefit from explicit technique practice. In-sessional learners need to fit proofreading into tight deadlines. Doctoral researchers proofread long documents, where consistency checks (terms, abbreviations, numbers, references) become more important than isolated errors.
reviewNotes: Evidence for specific proofreading techniques is largely practitioner-based; the single citation supports the self-editing rationale, not the techniques themselves.

guidance.summary: Sadler (1989) argued that learners can only improve if they hold a concept of the standard being aimed for, can compare their own work with it and can act to close the gap, and that exemplars are central to developing that concept. Andrade and Valtcheva (2009) describe rubric-referenced self-assessment as a means of promoting learning, and Nicol and Macfarlane-Dick (2006) place self-assessment at the centre of good feedback practice. Teach self-assessment repeatedly, with exemplars, and calibrate learners' judgements against tutors'.

activities.title: Criteria to questions
learnerActions: Rewrite each rubric criterion as two or three questions about a text
Apply them to an exemplar and then to your own draft
Mark the evidence in the text for each answer
activities.intendedInsight: Criteria become usable when turned into questions about specific features of the text.
activities.rationale: Reflects the rubric-referenced self-assessment process described by Andrade and Valtcheva (2009).

activities.title: Calibration
learnerActions: Grade two exemplars individually against the criteria
Compare with the tutor's grades and discuss the differences
Self-grade your own draft with evidence
activities.intendedInsight: Judgement of quality develops through comparison with expert judgements.
activities.rationale: Builds the concept of the standard that Sadler (1989) identified as a precondition for improvement.

difficulties.pattern: Self-assessment treated as box-ticking (‘yes, I have an introduction’).
difficulties.revealedBy: Every criterion ticked, with no evidence and no identified weakness.
difficulties.response: Require quoted evidence for each judgement and at least one identified weakness.

difficulties.pattern: Systematic over- or under-rating of one's own work.
difficulties.revealedBy: Large, consistent gaps between self-assigned and tutor grades.
difficulties.response: Use calibration tasks and discuss evidence rather than grades. Do not use self-assessment grades summatively.

diagnostic.task: Ask the learner to assess a supplied mid-band essay against a three-criterion rubric, then their own draft.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Judgements close to the tutor's, supported by quoted evidence, with a prioritised revision plan.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Reasonable overall judgement but little evidence, or no prioritisation.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Uniformly high or low judgements with no evidence.

guidance.contextNotes: Foundation learners need simplified criteria and frequent calibration. Pre-sessional programmes can build self-assessment into each draft submission. In-sessional learners should apply the process to their departments' own criteria, which vary considerably between disciplines.
reviewNotes: Overlaps with fbk.self-peer-assessment; this topic applies self-assessment specifically to revising drafts.

guidance.summary: Lundstrom and Baker (2009) found that L2 students trained to give peer feedback made greater gains in their own writing than those trained only to receive it, particularly on global aspects and among lower-proficiency students. Liu and Hansen (2002) and Min (2006) emphasise training: guided peer review with explicit criteria and modelling produces more useful comments and more revision. Hyland and Hyland (2019) review the social and affective dimensions of peer feedback. Train reviewers, structure the task, and focus early peer review on global issues.

activities.title: Reviewer training with a model draft
learnerActions: Review a model draft individually using a structured guidance sheet
Compare your comments with a tutor's model feedback
Rewrite your comments to make them specific and actionable
activities.intendedInsight: Useful feedback is specific, prioritised and explains why.
activities.rationale: Training reviewers with models and criteria is associated with more useful peer comments (Liu & Hansen, 2002; Min, 2006).

activities.title: Give to get
learnerActions: Review two peers' drafts
Write a note on one thing learned for your own draft
Revise your draft using that insight
activities.intendedInsight: Reviewing others' writing improves one's own.
activities.rationale: Draws on the finding that givers of peer feedback improved their own writing (Lundstrom & Baker, 2009).

difficulties.pattern: Comments limited to grammar and general praise (‘Good essay, some grammar mistakes’).
difficulties.revealedBy: Generic feedback sheets with no reference to argument or organisation.
difficulties.response: Provide structured guidance focused on global issues and model specific comments.

difficulties.pattern: ‘My classmates' English is no better than mine, so their feedback is useless.’
difficulties.revealedBy: Peer comments ignored in revision.
difficulties.response: Emphasise reader response and the benefits of reviewing, and combine peer feedback with tutor feedback.

difficulties.pattern: Avoiding any critical comment to protect relationships.
difficulties.revealedBy: Feedback consisting only of praise.
difficulties.response: Model mitigated critique (‘One thing that might strengthen this is…’) and make at least one suggestion compulsory.

diagnostic.task: Give a draft with one major global problem and ask for three written comments.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Identifies the global problem first, explains its effect on the reader and suggests a change, in a constructive tone.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Specific comments, but focused on local issues.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Generic praise or error lists.

guidance.contextNotes: Foundation learners need highly structured peer review and teacher modelling. Pre-sessional programmes can make peer review a regular part of drafting cycles. In-sessional and PGT learners may review across disciplines, focusing on clarity for non-specialist readers. Doctoral writing groups provide sustained peer review and lead into formal reviewing (see pub.peer-review-reports).
reviewNotes: min2006 is a proposed reference pending verification.

guidance.summary: Stevenson's (2016) synthesis of research on automated writing evaluation suggests that AWE feedback concentrates on surface features and is most useful when integrated into teaching rather than used in isolation. Lee (2020) reports that EFL students who used machine-translation output as a reference while revising reduced some lexicogrammatical errors, illustrating a potentially productive but rule-dependent use. Teach tools as one input among several, with explicit evaluation of each suggestion, and connect tool use to institutional rules on AI and integrity.

activities.title: Accept or reject
learnerActions: Run a paragraph through a grammar checker
Classify each suggestion as correct, wrong or meaning-changing
Verify uncertain suggestions with a learner dictionary or corpus
activities.intendedInsight: Tool suggestions need human judgement before they are accepted.
activities.rationale: Positions the tool as one source of feedback within teaching, consistent with Stevenson (2016).

activities.title: Policy check
learnerActions: Read the module or institutional rules on editing and AI tools
Classify five tool uses as permitted, permitted with disclosure, or not permitted
Discuss any uses the rules do not clearly cover
activities.intendedInsight: Permissions vary between contexts and must be checked for each assessment.
activities.rationale: Makes local rules explicit so that learners can use tools confidently and legitimately.

difficulties.pattern: Accepting every suggestion the tool makes.
difficulties.revealedBy: New errors and changes of meaning introduced at the final stage.
difficulties.response: Use the accept-or-reject task and require learners to justify rejections.

difficulties.pattern: Using AI rewriting tools to ‘improve’ whole paragraphs.
difficulties.revealedBy: Shifts in voice, drift in meaning, unfamiliar vocabulary the learner cannot explain.
difficulties.response: Discuss rules, authorship and voice, and show how meaning can drift; restrict tools to targeted checks where required.

diagnostic.task: Give a paragraph with ten tool suggestions and ask the learner to decide on each in five minutes.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Correct decisions on most suggestions, rejections justified, meaning-changing suggestion identified.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Mostly correct but accepts the meaning-changing suggestion.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Accepts all suggestions or rejects all without reasons.

guidance.contextNotes: Foundation and pre-sessional learners need explicit guidance on what tools can and cannot do and on local rules. In-sessional learners face varied module policies. Doctoral researchers must also consider confidentiality when uploading unpublished work to online tools (see gai.privacy-ip).
reviewNotes: Overlaps with dig.automated-feedback-tools and gai.language-support. Tool capabilities and institutional rules change rapidly; guidance is deliberately general.

guidance.summary: Harwood, Austin and Macaulay (2009) found wide variation in what proofreaders of student writing at a UK university did, ranging from correcting surface errors to intervening substantially in content, which shows why clear policies and learner awareness matter. Lillis and Curry (2010) describe how ‘literacy brokers’ shape multilingual scholars' publications, making editorial help a normal part of research publication. Teach the local policy, discuss grey areas openly, and avoid implying that seeking legitimate help is itself dishonest.

activities.title: Policy sorting
learnerActions: Read a sample institutional proofreading policy
Classify a list of interventions as permitted or not
Discuss the grey areas and how to resolve them
activities.intendedInsight: Policies draw a line between surface correction and changes to content and argument.
activities.rationale: Variation in proofreaders' practices (Harwood et al., 2009) means learners must know where their own institution draws the line.

activities.title: Briefing a proofreader
learnerActions: Write a short brief specifying which changes a proofreader may make
Plan how changes will be recorded, for example using tracked changes
activities.intendedInsight: Writers are responsible for controlling and documenting the help they receive.
activities.rationale: Transparency about third-party input protects the writer and clarifies authorship.

difficulties.pattern: ‘A friend only improved my English, so it is still my work.’
difficulties.revealedBy: The learner's own account of what the helper changed; tracked changes or earlier drafts showing content-level rewriting. Style differences between supervised and submitted writing are not evidence on their own.
difficulties.response: Discuss where improving language becomes changing content and authorship, using concrete examples.

difficulties.pattern: Fear that any help is cheating, leading learners to avoid legitimate support.
difficulties.revealedBy: Non-use of writing centres and in-sessional tutorials.
difficulties.response: Show permitted routes to support and what each offers.

diagnostic.task: Give three scenarios of third-party help (a friend rewrites a paragraph, a paid proofreader corrects spelling, an AI tool restructures an essay) and ask whether each is permitted under a sample policy.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Classifies each correctly with reasons referring to the content/surface distinction and disclosure.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Classifies correctly but cannot explain the principle.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Treats all help as acceptable, or all as cheating.

guidance.contextNotes: Foundation and pre-sessional learners need clear institutional rules, especially where progression depends on assessed writing. In-sessional learners may be tempted by paid services under pressure. Doctoral researchers need to know thesis regulations on editorial help, which often differ from coursework rules, and norms of professional editing for publication.
reviewNotes: harwood2009 is a proposed reference pending verification. Institutional policies vary; guidance does not prescribe a single standard.

guidance.summary: Wingate (2012) found that students often understood essay writing as structuring content rather than presenting an argument, and argued for explicit teaching of argument as the organising principle. The five-paragraph essay can introduce thesis-led structure, but contributors to Caplan and Johns (2019) argue that it misrepresents university writing, and Nesi and Gardner (2012) show how much essays vary across disciplines. Teach structure as argument mapping and use authentic student essays from target disciplines as models.

activities.title: Argument map of a model essay
learnerActions: Write the thesis of a high-scoring student essay in one sentence
Write one sentence per body paragraph stating its contribution to the thesis
Draw arrows showing how the points build on each other
activities.intendedInsight: An essay's structure is its argument laid out in order.
activities.rationale: Makes argument the organising principle, as Wingate (2012) recommends, rather than a sequence of content blocks.

activities.title: Template versus university essay
learnerActions: Compare a five-paragraph test-style essay with a 2,000-word university essay on a similar topic
List differences in length, sources, paragraphing and structure
Decide what from the five-paragraph model is worth keeping
activities.intendedInsight: The template teaches thesis-led organisation but not how university essays actually work.
activities.rationale: Explicit comparison helps learners keep what transfers and discard what does not (Caplan & Johns, 2019).

difficulties.pattern: ‘An essay has five paragraphs: an introduction, three body paragraphs and a conclusion.’
difficulties.revealedBy: Three-point essays regardless of length; padding to fit the template.
difficulties.response: Show essays of varying structure and plan from the argument. Do not simply forbid the template; explain what it gets right and where it stops being useful.

difficulties.pattern: Structure follows the order of the sources or a list of topics rather than the argument.
difficulties.revealedBy: Body paragraphs that each summarise one reading or describe one topic.
difficulties.response: Use argument-mapping tasks and thesis-led planning.

diagnostic.task: Ask the learner to outline an essay for a ‘to what extent’ question.
diagnostic.strongResponse: A thesis containing a judgement; body sections ordered to build a case, including a counter-argument and response; a conclusion that answers ‘to what extent’.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Thesis present, but the body is balanced for and against without building to the judgement.
diagnostic.gapResponse: A list of topics with no thesis.

guidance.contextNotes: Foundation programmes may begin with structured templates. Pre-sessional programmes should move learners to argument-driven structure in extended essays, with explicit discussion of how university essays differ from test essays.

guidance.summary: A thesis is the textual realisation of a position; Wingate (2012) identifies developing and stating a position as a core component of argument that students find difficult. Andrews (2010) treats argument in higher education as a mode of thinking that needs explicit teaching rather than being left implicit. Teach thesis statements by contrast (fact, announcement, opinion, arguable claim), insist on revising the thesis after drafting, and acknowledge that some disciplines and essay types favour an exploratory or delayed thesis.

activities.title: Thesis ladder
learnerActions: Start from a topic announcement
Add a position, then reasons, then a qualification
Judge which version best suits a 1,500-word essay
activities.intendedInsight: Arguable, qualified theses are both stronger and easier to support.
activities.rationale: Stepwise transformation makes the components of a position explicit (Wingate, 2012).

activities.title: Thesis–essay match
learnerActions: Read a model essay with its thesis removed
Write the thesis the essay actually argues
Compare with the original thesis and with the essay question
activities.intendedInsight: The thesis must match what the essay does, which may differ from the writer's original plan.
activities.rationale: Encourages treating the thesis as a claim to be revised in the light of the argument (Andrews, 2010).

difficulties.pattern: ‘This essay will discuss the advantages and disadvantages of X.’
difficulties.revealedBy: Announcements with no position; descriptive essays.
difficulties.response: Explain that announcements can serve as roadmaps but are not theses, and require a separate position sentence.

difficulties.pattern: Avoiding a clear position because it feels presumptuous or risky.
difficulties.revealedBy: Heavily hedged or evenly balanced theses (‘there are both advantages and disadvantages’).
difficulties.response: Show theses that are clear but qualified and discuss what markers reward.

difficulties.pattern: Overbroad theses that cannot be supported within the word limit.
difficulties.revealedBy: Superficial treatment of many points; sweeping generalisations.
difficulties.response: Practise scoping the thesis with qualification and limiting conditions (context, period, population).

diagnostic.task: Give a question and ask for a thesis in one or two sentences.
diagnostic.strongResponse: A clear, arguable, qualified position that answers the question and is feasible in scope.
diagnostic.partialResponse: A position is present but overbroad or not quite answering the question as set.
diagnostic.gapResponse: A topic announcement or a statement of fact.

guidance.contextNotes: Foundation learners can start from opinion-based theses and move to source-based ones. Pre-sessional and undergraduate in-sessional learners need theses that answer specific disciplinary questions. PGT writers need theses that take a position within a scholarly debate, and may meet disciplinary preferences for where and how explicitly the thesis is stated.
reviewNotes: Some disciplines and essay types favour a thesis that emerges towards the end; this topic presents an explicit early thesis as a default rather than a rule.

guidance.summary: Essay introductions typically move from general to specific, a pattern Swales and Feak (2012) describe for many academic texts; research-article introductions (the CARS model) are related but distinct (see res.introductions-cars). Frame markers and roadmaps help readers (Hyland, 2005), but their density should suit the length of the text and the discipline. Teach introductions as something finalised last, and analyse them in authentic student essays rather than textbook formulas.

activities.title: Introduction move analysis
learnerActions: Label the moves in three high-scoring student introductions
Estimate the proportion of words in each move
Draft an introduction for your own essay using similar proportions
activities.intendedInsight: Effective introductions spend little space on background and reach the thesis quickly.
activities.rationale: Move analysis of exemplars builds genre awareness of general–specific organisation (Swales & Feak, 2012).

activities.title: Opening repair
learnerActions: Collect weak openings (sweeping generalisation, dictionary definition, rhetorical question)
Rewrite each as a specific, relevant opening
Discuss when an opening definition is justified by the question
activities.intendedInsight: A specific opening signals focus from the first sentence.
activities.rationale: Targets formulaic openings that markers frequently criticise and links to work on vague and overgeneralised language.

difficulties.pattern: Opening with sweeping generalisations (‘Nowadays, technology is very important in our lives’) or dictionary definitions.
difficulties.revealedBy: Generic first sentences that could introduce almost any essay.
difficulties.response: Rewrite openings to name a specific context, debate or problem (see reg.vague-overgeneralised).

difficulties.pattern: Long background that delays the thesis.
difficulties.revealedBy: Introductions taking a fifth or more of the essay; the thesis appears on the second page.
difficulties.response: Word-budget the introduction and move necessary background into the body.

difficulties.pattern: Roadmaps that promise a structure the essay does not follow.
difficulties.revealedBy: Mismatch between the roadmap and the order of body sections.
difficulties.response: Finalise the introduction after the body is drafted and check the roadmap against the topic sentences.

diagnostic.task: Ask for a 100–150-word introduction to a supplied essay plan.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Specific context, efficient narrowing, a clear thesis and a brief roadmap consistent with the plan.
diagnostic.partialResponse: All elements present, but background is too long or the thesis is vague.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Background only, or no thesis.

guidance.contextNotes: Foundation learners can use a general-to-specific template. Pre-sessional and in-sessional learners should compare disciplinary variation: some fields expect definitions of key terms, others discourage roadmaps in short essays. PGT writers often need to justify their chosen focus in the introduction.

guidance.summary: The conclusion is where the position is stated in full; Wingate (2012) found that students' understanding of argument often stopped at presenting points rather than reaching a judgement. Teach the difference between summary and synthesis and the value of stating implications and limits, and connect conclusions to claim calibration so that they neither overclaim nor retreat into vagueness. Andrews (2010) treats reaching a reasoned conclusion as integral to argument rather than an afterthought.

activities.title: Summary versus synthesis
learnerActions: Compare two conclusions to the same essay
Identify which explains how the points relate to the answer
Rewrite the summary-style conclusion as a synthesis
activities.intendedInsight: Synthesis states what the points show together, not just what they were.
activities.rationale: Makes the argumentative function of the conclusion explicit (Wingate, 2012).

activities.title: Answer, qualify, extend
learnerActions: Write one sentence that answers the question directly
Write one that qualifies the answer in the light of the evidence
Write one that states an implication or a question for further work
activities.intendedInsight: A short three-move conclusion can be complete and well calibrated.
activities.rationale: Provides a flexible structure that foregrounds judgement and calibration rather than repetition.

difficulties.pattern: ‘In conclusion, there are both advantages and disadvantages.’
difficulties.revealedBy: Conclusions with no judgement; the question is never actually answered.
difficulties.response: Require a direct-answer sentence and check it against the thesis.

difficulties.pattern: Introducing new evidence or new arguments in the conclusion.
difficulties.revealedBy: New citations or claims in the final paragraph.
difficulties.response: Check every sentence of the conclusion against the body; move new material into the body or cut it.

difficulties.pattern: Overclaiming (‘This essay has proved that…’).
difficulties.revealedBy: Strong boosters in the conclusion after limited or mixed evidence.
difficulties.response: Link to claim calibration and ask learners to justify the strength of the final claim.

diagnostic.task: Give a three-paragraph essay body and ask for a conclusion of about 100 words.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Direct, calibrated answer; synthesis of how the points combine; one implication or limitation; no new evidence.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Answers the question but summarises points in sequence, or omits limitations.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Repeats the introduction, lists points without an answer, or introduces new material.

guidance.contextNotes: Foundation and pre-sessional learners focus on summary versus synthesis and giving a direct answer. In-sessional undergraduates add implications and limitations. PGT writers increasingly use conclusions to position their argument within a wider debate.

guidance.summary: Hoey (1983) shows how texts are organised through recurring patterns such as problem–solution and general–particular, which offer ordering principles beyond ‘firstly, secondly, thirdly’. Spivey (1990) identifies organising as a central operation in writing from sources, and source-by-source organisation is a default for many learners. Wingate (2012) argues that organisation should be driven by the argument, so teach ordering as a decision justified by the thesis.

activities.title: Re-sort the body
learnerActions: Cut a source-by-source draft into sentence strips
Regroup the strips by theme and write a claim for each group
Order the groups and justify the order in relation to the thesis
activities.intendedInsight: Thematic organisation exposes relationships between sources and supports an argument.
activities.rationale: Physically regrouping material enacts the organising operation of discourse synthesis (Spivey, 1990).

activities.title: Pattern choice
learnerActions: Identify the organising pattern (problem–solution, comparison, cause–effect, concession–rebuttal) in three model essays
Choose a pattern for a new question and justify it
activities.intendedInsight: Different questions call for different organising patterns.
activities.rationale: Text patterns provide principled ordering options (Hoey, 1983).

difficulties.pattern: Source-by-source organisation, with one paragraph per author.
difficulties.revealedBy: Body paragraphs that each summarise one reading.
difficulties.response: Use re-sorting tasks and a simple synthesis grid before drafting.

difficulties.pattern: Points appear in the order they occurred to the writer.
difficulties.revealedBy: Weak points first and strongest buried; counter-argument placed at the end without a response.
difficulties.response: Ask learners to state and justify their ordering principle, and check it with a reverse outline.

diagnostic.task: Give a question and six points with their sources; ask for an ordered outline.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Points grouped thematically and ordered by a stated rationale; counter-argument positioned and answered.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Logical order overall, but some grouping by source remains.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Points listed in the order given or grouped by source.

guidance.contextNotes: Foundation learners need a small set of ordering principles. Pre-sessional learners should practise thematic organisation of sources in extended essays. Undergraduate and PGT in-sessional learners meet disciplinary organising patterns and longer essays divided into sections.

guidance.summary: Relevance is defined by the task, and tutors' comments about ‘answering the question’ are frequent but often opaque to students (Lea & Street, 1998). Wingate (2012) links relevance to argument: material is relevant when it advances the position the essay takes on the question. Teach checking routines based on the thesis and topic sentences, and show how the same content can be relevant or irrelevant depending on how it is framed.

activities.title: Relevance audit
learnerActions: Write the question at the top of the draft
For each paragraph, write one line in the margin on how it helps answer the question
Decide to keep, reframe or cut each paragraph
activities.intendedInsight: Every paragraph has to earn its place by advancing the answer.
activities.rationale: Makes tacit expectations about relevance explicit (Lea & Street, 1998).

activities.title: Reframe, don't remove
learnerActions: Take a descriptive paragraph from a draft
Rewrite its first and last sentences so that it connects to the question
Decide whether the reframing works or the paragraph should go
activities.intendedInsight: Relevance is often a matter of framing as well as content.
activities.rationale: Connects relevance with argument (Wingate, 2012).

difficulties.pattern: Writing about the topic rather than the question.
difficulties.revealedBy: Generic essays; marker comments such as ‘relevance?’.
difficulties.response: Use relevance audits and question-focused topic sentences. Do not tell learners to repeat the question's wording in every paragraph, which produces mechanical text without improving relevance.

difficulties.pattern: Answering one part of a multi-part question at length and neglecting the other.
difficulties.revealedBy: Unbalanced essays in which the evaluative part of the question receives a single paragraph.
difficulties.response: Word-budget each part of the question at the planning stage.

diagnostic.task: Give a question and three paragraphs on the same topic; ask which is most relevant and why.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Judges relevance by contribution to the answer and suggests how to reframe the weaker paragraphs.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Judges relevance by topic overlap with the question.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Judges by length, number of sources or quality of English.

guidance.contextNotes: At foundation level the focus is on matching paragraphs to questions. In pre-sessional extended essays, drift from the question often increases as more sources are added. In-sessional learners face disciplinary questions with complex limits, and PGT students frequently set their own questions, which then have to be answered consistently.

guidance.summary: Nesi and Gardner (2012) identify the essay as one of thirteen genre families in British university student writing, with subtypes including exposition, discussion, factorial and challenge essays (Gardner & Nesi, 2013). Moore and Morton (2005) show that test essays differ from university essays, notably in drawing on personal opinion rather than sources. Teach essay types as purposes rather than formulas, and make clear that labels in textbooks and course handbooks vary.

activities.title: Same topic, different type
learnerActions: Read four questions on one topic
Identify the type and purpose implied by each
Write a thesis for each and compare how they differ
activities.intendedInsight: The essay type determines what the thesis has to do.
activities.rationale: Holding the topic constant isolates the effect of purpose, using the genre-family categories of Gardner and Nesi (2013).

activities.title: Decode real questions
learnerActions: Collect essay questions from target departments
Classify them using essay-family subtypes
Note questions that blend types and discuss how to plan for them
activities.intendedInsight: Real questions often blend types; classification is a planning aid, not a rule.
activities.rationale: Authentic questions reveal disciplinary variation (Nesi & Gardner, 2012).

difficulties.pattern: ‘Discuss means present both sides without taking a view.’
difficulties.revealedBy: Balanced essays that end without a judgement.
difficulties.response: Show high-scoring discussion essays that weigh perspectives and reach a reasoned conclusion.

difficulties.pattern: Applying proficiency-test essay types to university questions.
difficulties.revealedBy: Opinion essays based on personal experience with no sources.
difficulties.response: Compare test and university essays explicitly, drawing on Moore and Morton (2005), and discuss what each rewards.

diagnostic.task: Give three questions and ask the learner to name the essay type each implies and outline its structure in three lines.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Types identified with reference to purpose; outlines differ appropriately, and any blended question is recognised.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Types identified from command words, but outlines are nearly identical.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Same five-paragraph outline offered for all three.

guidance.contextNotes: Foundation learners need the main types. Pre-sessional programmes should address unlearning test-essay habits. In-sessional learners meet disciplinary types such as legal essays (see dlw.legal-essays) and interpretive essays (see dhu.interpretive-argument).
reviewNotes: Overlaps with the GES genre topics (for example ges.argumentative-essay, ges.discussion-essay); this topic provides the conceptual overview, and the genre topics cover production of each type.

guidance.summary: Headings are a genre convention: they are standard in reports and related genre families (Gardner & Nesi, 2013) and specified in style guides such as APA (American Psychological Association, 2020), but discouraged in some essay traditions. Teach learners to check local expectations, to write informative rather than generic headings, and to keep the prose coherent without relying on headings.

activities.title: Headings test
learnerActions: Remove the headings from a draft
Read it for coherence and add transitions where needed
Restore informative headings only if they are permitted and helpful
activities.intendedInsight: Headings support coherent prose but do not replace it.
activities.rationale: Prevents headings from substituting for topic sentences and transitions.

activities.title: Generic to informative
learnerActions: Rewrite a set of generic headings as informative headings
Compare with headings in published articles in the learner's field
activities.intendedInsight: Informative headings preview content and argument.
activities.rationale: Style guidance recommends descriptive headings in a consistent hierarchy (American Psychological Association, 2020).

difficulties.pattern: Using report-style headings in essays where the discipline discourages them.
difficulties.revealedBy: Headed essays in modules whose guidance asks for continuous prose.
difficulties.response: Have learners check local guidance or ask the tutor before deciding.

difficulties.pattern: Headings replace topic sentences and transitions.
difficulties.revealedBy: Abrupt section openings; the text is hard to follow without its headings.
difficulties.response: Use the headings test and require a linking sentence at the start of each section.

diagnostic.task: Ask whether headings are appropriate for two given assignment briefs and, for one, write headings for a supplied outline.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Decision based on brief and discipline; informative headings in a consistent hierarchy.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Reasonable decision, but generic headings.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Uses or omits headings without reference to the brief; headings inconsistent.

guidance.contextNotes: Pre-sessional learners should meet both headed and unheaded essays. In-sessional undergraduates need disciplinary conventions. PGT essays are often longer and more likely to permit headings, but expectations still vary by department.

guidance.summary: Bereiter and Scardamalia (1987) describe knowledge-telling as writing down what one knows about a topic, which naturally produces breadth; knowledge-transforming involves selecting and reworking content to meet goals. Teach narrowing as a strategic choice, model explicit scope statements, and show how depth is achieved by layering analysis rather than adding points. This supports the argument-centred view of essays advocated by Wingate (2012).

activities.title: Cut to three
learnerActions: List all possible points for a question
Choose the three that best support the thesis
Plan four layers of development for one of them
activities.intendedInsight: Fewer points developed in depth usually make a stronger essay.
activities.rationale: Selecting for a goal is a hallmark of knowledge-transforming rather than knowledge-telling (Bereiter & Scardamalia, 1987).

activities.title: Scope statement
learnerActions: Write a sentence for the introduction stating what the essay focuses on and why
Write one acknowledging what it will not cover
activities.intendedInsight: An explicit scope shows control rather than omission.
activities.rationale: A justified focus is a visible sign of argumentative control (Wingate, 2012).

difficulties.pattern: ‘If I leave something out, the marker will think I don't know it.’
difficulties.revealedBy: Long lists of points, each treated superficially.
difficulties.response: Show exemplar feedback that rewards depth, and practise scope statements.

difficulties.pattern: Taking a very broad question literally (all countries, all periods, all theories).
difficulties.revealedBy: Generalised claims with little specific evidence.
difficulties.response: Narrow to cases or contexts and justify the choice in the introduction.

diagnostic.task: Give a broad question and ask for a one-paragraph plan stating focus, rationale and the points to be covered within 1,500 words.
diagnostic.strongResponse: A defensible narrowed focus with a rationale, three or four points, and an acknowledgement of what is excluded.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Some narrowing, but still too many points or no rationale.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Attempts to cover the whole question with many points.

guidance.contextNotes: Some pre-sessional learners face the opposite problem of having too little to say, which calls for work on development rather than narrowing. Undergraduates frequently need help narrowing broad questions. PGT writers need to scope essays in relation to the literature and justify their focus.

guidance.summary: Moore (2013) found that academics define critical thinking in several distinct ways, so ‘criticality’ should be unpacked in relation to the discipline and task rather than taught as a single generic skill; its teachability and cultural framing have also been questioned in TESOL (Atkinson, 1997). Lancaster (2014) identified stance patterns valued in high-graded upper-level student writing, such as entertaining alternatives and conceding before countering, which give criticality a recognisable linguistic form. Teach criticality by contrasting descriptive and critical versions of the same paragraph and by making the language of evaluation explicit.

activities.title: Describe, analyse, evaluate
learnerActions: Label the sentences of two paragraphs as description, analysis or evaluation
Rewrite the description-heavy paragraph to add analysis and evaluation
Compare with a high-scoring exemplar
activities.intendedInsight: Criticality is visible in specific sentence functions, not a vague quality.
activities.rationale: Operationalises an otherwise opaque criterion and links it to argument (Wingate, 2012).

activities.title: Concede and counter
learnerActions: Identify concession–counter patterns in an expert or high-graded essay
Write a paragraph that concedes a limitation of your own position and then responds to it
activities.intendedInsight: Acknowledging alternatives strengthens rather than weakens a position.
activities.rationale: Such patterns are characteristic of valued student writing in the disciplines (Lancaster, 2014).

difficulties.pattern: ‘Being critical means criticising.’
difficulties.revealedBy: Wholly negative evaluations; strengths of sources never acknowledged.
difficulties.response: Present criticality as balanced, reasoned judgement and model praise–criticism pairs.

difficulties.pattern: Reluctance to evaluate published authors or lecturers.
difficulties.revealedBy: Neutral reporting with no evaluation even when the question asks for it.
difficulties.response: Show mitigated evaluative language and explain what markers expect. Many learners from many backgrounds share this hesitation, so avoid attributing it to any national or cultural group.

difficulties.pattern: Criticality expressed as unsupported opinion (‘I think this theory is wrong’).
difficulties.revealedBy: Evaluations with no reasons or evidence.
difficulties.response: Require a reason and evidence for every evaluative claim, and link to evaluating evidence in reading.

diagnostic.task: Give a descriptive paragraph summarising two studies and ask the learner to make it critical in no more than 80 additional words.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Adds evaluation of evidence or method, a comparison of the studies and a judgement tied to the essay's argument.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Adds evaluation, but it is generic (‘this study has limitations’) or unconnected to the argument.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Adds more description, or adds unsupported opinion.

guidance.contextNotes: Pre-sessional programmes typically focus on evaluating sources and making a position visible. Undergraduate in-sessional work should address disciplinary forms of criticality, which differ across fields; even within the humanities, Moore (2013) found academics in history, philosophy and cultural studies holding distinct conceptions of critical thinking. PGT writers are expected to engage critically with debates and methods.
reviewNotes: The concept of criticality is contested; this topic adopts a working, discipline-sensitive definition rather than claiming a single construct.

guidance.summary: Swales and Feak (2012) treat titles as a short but consequential part of academic texts that should signal the focus of the work, and style guides such as APA (American Psychological Association, 2020) specify title format and capitalisation. Teach titles as a revision task—written or confirmed last, checked against the thesis, and compared with titles in the target discipline.

activities.title: Title from thesis
learnerActions: Write three titles for an essay from its thesis: a descriptive title, an argumentative title and a colon title
Ask peers which best predicts the essay's content and position
activities.intendedInsight: A good title predicts the content, and sometimes the argument.
activities.rationale: Links the title to the thesis and to reader expectations (Swales & Feak, 2012).

activities.title: Disciplinary title survey
learnerActions: Collect ten article titles from a journal in your field
Classify their structures (descriptive, question, colon, statement of finding)
Write a title for your own work in the most common style
activities.intendedInsight: Title conventions vary across fields.
activities.rationale: Small-scale genre analysis of authentic titles develops independent awareness of disciplinary norms.

difficulties.pattern: Using the essay question, the module code or a single word as the title.
difficulties.revealedBy: Titles such as ‘Essay 2’ or ‘Globalisation’.
difficulties.response: Use the title-from-thesis task.

difficulties.pattern: Inconsistent capitalisation of titles and headings.
difficulties.revealedBy: Mixed sentence case and title case within one document.
difficulties.response: Teach the convention of the required style and check it during proofreading.

diagnostic.task: Give an essay abstract or thesis and ask for a title.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Specific, concise title indicating topic and focus (and, where appropriate, position), correctly capitalised.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Accurate topic but no indication of focus, or overlong.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Vague one- or two-word title, or the question copied.

guidance.contextNotes: Foundation learners usually receive set titles. Undergraduate and PGT writers need titles for self-chosen essays, projects and dissertations. At PGR level, titles of articles, theses and conference abstracts affect discoverability and should reflect disciplinary conventions.

guidance.summary: The one-idea paragraph is a well-established pedagogical model and a helpful default for reading and writing, but Braddock's (1974) analysis of professional expository prose found that many paragraphs did not open with an explicit topic sentence, and some had none. Present the model as a reader-friendly convention rather than a law, and use authentic academic paragraphs alongside textbook models. Swales and Feak (2012) show how paragraphs organise information (for example general–specific), which is useful for awareness-raising.

activities.title: Paragraph jigsaw
learnerActions: Sort sentences from two shuffled paragraphs on related topics into two paragraphs
State each paragraph's controlling idea in one sentence
Explain which clues (point, reference, logic) guided the sorting
activities.intendedInsight: Paragraph unity comes from a shared point, not merely shared vocabulary.
activities.rationale: Reconstruction makes unity and its signals noticeable before learners have to produce it.

activities.title: Textbook versus published paragraphs
learnerActions: Compare a textbook model paragraph with two paragraphs from published work in the learner's field
Locate the main point in each
Discuss why the published writers placed it where they did
activities.intendedInsight: The one-idea principle holds widely, but where the main point is placed varies with function.
activities.rationale: Contrasting idealised and authentic paragraphs guards against overgeneralising from textbook models (Braddock, 1974).

difficulties.pattern: Paragraphs drift because each sentence follows from the one before rather than from the controlling idea.
difficulties.revealedBy: Final sentences unrelated to the first; readers unable to summarise the paragraph.
difficulties.response: Ask learners to note the paragraph's point in the margin before drafting and again after, and to compare the two.

difficulties.pattern: ‘A paragraph is five sentences’ or ‘I start a new paragraph whenever I use However’.
difficulties.revealedBy: Uniform paragraph lengths; breaks at connectors rather than at changes of point.
difficulties.response: Discuss paragraphing as a decision about points, and show variation in authentic texts.

diagnostic.task: Give an unparagraphed 300-word text containing three points and ask for paragraph breaks plus a one-line label for each paragraph.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Breaks match changes of point; labels state the point (a claim), not merely the topic.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Breaks mostly correct, but labels are topics, or one break is driven by length.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Breaks at arbitrary points or before every connector.

guidance.contextNotes: Foundation and early pre-sessional learners benefit most from explicit work on unity. By the later stages of a pre-sessional programme, authentic disciplinary paragraphs should be used to show legitimate variation.
reviewNotes: Braddock (1974) analysed edited professional essays, not student academic writing; it is cited to qualify the universality of the topic-sentence model, not to dismiss the model. braddock1974 is a proposed reference.

guidance.summary: Teach topic sentences as claims that make a promise the rest of the paragraph keeps; prediction tasks are a quick test of whether a topic sentence is doing this. Reading a text's topic sentences in sequence is also a powerful check on the overall argument (see edt.reverse-outlining) and connects paragraph work to Wingate's (2012) emphasis on argument. Because expert writers do not always put the main point first (Braddock, 1974), present first-sentence topic sentences as a strong default rather than a rule.

activities.title: Fact, topic or claim?
learnerActions: Classify a set of paragraph openings as facts, topic announcements or claims
Rewrite the facts and announcements as claims
Predict the content of the paragraph that would follow each claim
activities.intendedInsight: A good topic sentence lets a reader predict the paragraph.
activities.rationale: Prediction operationalises the promise function of topic sentences and exposes vague controlling ideas.

activities.title: Topic-sentence spine
learnerActions: Extract the topic sentences of a model essay and read them in sequence
Do the same with one's own draft
Revise any topic sentence that does not advance the argument
activities.intendedInsight: Together, topic sentences form the skeleton of the argument.
activities.rationale: Linking paragraph-level and text-level structure supports the shift from description to argument (Wingate, 2012).

difficulties.pattern: Topic sentences that are too broad (‘Technology has changed society’) or too narrow (a single statistic).
difficulties.revealedBy: Paragraphs that cannot fulfil their opening, or have nowhere to go after it.
difficulties.response: Practise scaling controlling ideas with general and shell nouns (‘two main factors’, ‘a significant limitation’) and test them with prediction.

difficulties.pattern: Opening with a source (‘Smith (2019) states that…’), so that the source rather than the writer controls the paragraph.
difficulties.revealedBy: Paragraphs that summarise one source with no point of the writer's own.
difficulties.response: Ask learners to begin with their own claim and move the citation into the support.

diagnostic.task: Give a paragraph body without its first sentence and ask for a topic sentence.
diagnostic.strongResponse: A claim of suitable scope that the body supports, framed with a controlling noun or phrase and linked to the wider argument.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Accurate topic but no claim, or a claim somewhat broader than the content.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Repeats a detail from the body or offers an unrelated generalisation.

guidance.contextNotes: At foundation level, insist on explicit topic sentences as the default. In pre-sessional and in-sessional work, extend to linking topic sentences to the thesis and varying their placement. In undergraduate disciplinary writing, topic sentences increasingly carry synthesis and evaluation across sources.

guidance.summary: Toulmin's (2003) model makes visible what a supported claim needs: grounds, and the warrant linking them to the claim. Hoey's (1983) general–particular and matching patterns describe how support is typically organised in text, and Andrews (2010) argues that argumentation in higher education needs explicit teaching. Teach support as a repertoire—explanation, data, example, comparison, concession—chosen to fit the claim, with particular emphasis on the explanatory sentences that learners most often omit.

activities.title: Support-type audit
learnerActions: Colour-code the sentences of a model paragraph by function (claim, explanation, evidence, example, comment)
Do the same for one of your own paragraphs
Add the missing function, which is usually explanation or comment
activities.intendedInsight: Strong paragraphs mix kinds of support and state the link between evidence and claim.
activities.rationale: Functional analysis makes Toulmin-style grounds and warrants visible at sentence level (Toulmin, 2003).

activities.title: Is that enough?
learnerActions: In groups, judge whether given evidence is sufficient for three claims of different strength
Either weaken over-strong claims or add evidence
Explain each decision to another group
activities.intendedInsight: How much support is needed, and of what kind, depends on how strong the claim is.
activities.rationale: Connects paragraph development to the evaluation of arguments, which Andrews (2010) treats as central to higher-education argumentation.

difficulties.pattern: A single example is presented as if it proves a general claim.
difficulties.revealedBy: One anecdote or case per paragraph; ‘For example…’ followed by the end of the paragraph.
difficulties.response: Distinguish illustration from evidence and ask ‘how typical is this example, and how do we know?’

difficulties.pattern: Claim plus quotation, with no explanation of how the quotation supports the claim.
difficulties.revealedBy: Quotations ending paragraphs; tutor comments such as ‘so what?’ or ‘explain’.
difficulties.response: Require at least one sentence of the writer's own explanation after each piece of evidence.

diagnostic.task: Ask the learner to write a paragraph supporting a given claim using one supplied data point and one example.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Claim, data, explanation of its significance, example with comment and, if needed, a qualification of the claim.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Data and example included, but the explanation is thin or merely restates them.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Restates the claim, or lists the data and the example with no link to the claim.

guidance.contextNotes: Foundation writers often rely on personal examples and general knowledge, which suits some tasks but needs to move towards source-based evidence. Pre-sessional programmes introduce evidence from reading. In-sessional undergraduates need a disciplinary sense of what counts as evidence (see acu.disciplinary-knowledge).

guidance.summary: PEEL and similar acronyms are widely used in schools and foundation programmes because they make paragraph functions explicit. Wingate (2012) argues that essay advice focused on structure can obscure the purpose of essays, which is argument, and contributors to Caplan and Johns (2019) critique formulaic templates such as the five-paragraph essay for producing text that does not transfer to university genres. Use PEEL as a scaffold that is explicitly withdrawn over time, in the spirit of the guided-to-independent sequence in Sydney School genre pedagogy (Rose & Martin, 2012), and compare scaffolded with authentic paragraphs early.

activities.title: PEEL and beyond
learnerActions: Label a PEEL model paragraph
Label two authentic paragraphs from the target discipline using the same scheme
List what the authentic paragraphs do that PEEL does not capture
activities.intendedInsight: PEEL names useful functions but not a fixed order or number of moves.
activities.rationale: Comparing a scaffold with authentic text builds genre awareness rather than template-following (Caplan & Johns, 2019).

activities.title: Fade the scaffold
learnerActions: Write one paragraph with PEEL labels in the margin
Write the next with only a margin note of the point
Write a third with no notes and ask a partner to identify the functions
activities.intendedInsight: The functions can be internalised and then used flexibly.
activities.rationale: Moving from supported to independent construction reflects the teaching–learning cycle of genre pedagogy (Rose & Martin, 2012).

difficulties.pattern: ‘Every paragraph must be PEEL, and the last sentence must link back to the question.’
difficulties.revealedBy: Repetitive link sentences (‘This shows that X is important for the question’).
difficulties.response: Show authentic paragraphs without link sentences and discuss when a link is needed. Do not ban PEEL abruptly; reframe it as one option among several.

difficulties.pattern: One piece of evidence per paragraph, whatever the claim.
difficulties.revealedBy: Under-supported claims; no comparison of sources within a paragraph.
difficulties.response: Introduce paragraphs that combine several sources and relate support to claim strength.

diagnostic.task: Ask the learner to write a paragraph making one point supported by two sources that partly disagree.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Point, both sources integrated with their relationship stated, explanation and a qualified conclusion; the structure departs from PEEL where needed.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Uses PEEL rigidly, with two separate evidence–explanation blocks and a formulaic link.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Cannot accommodate the second source or the disagreement; only one source is summarised.

guidance.contextNotes: PEEL is most useful at foundation and early pre-sessional stages, especially for learners whose schooling used it. By the end of a pre-sessional programme, learners should treat it as one option. Some learners arriving in in-sessional classes have to unlearn rigid PEEL in disciplines that value other paragraph patterns.
reviewNotes: No published study known to the author tests PEEL specifically; the critique draws on broader work on formulaic writing instruction. caplanjohns2019 is a proposed reference.

guidance.summary: Daneš (1974) described how themes progress across sentences, and Halliday and Hasan (1976) catalogued the cohesive ties that connect them; Swales and Feak (2012) turn these ideas into practical advice on old-to-new flow. Crossley and McNamara (2012) found that measures of explicit cohesion did not predict higher proficiency ratings of L2 essays in the way often assumed, whereas lexical sophistication did, which supports teaching information flow and logic rather than connector density. Work with learners' own paragraphs and focus on sentence openings.

activities.title: Theme tracking
learnerActions: Underline the first noun phrase of each sentence in a paragraph
Draw an arrow from each to where that information first appeared
Rewrite sentences whose openings have no backward link
activities.intendedInsight: Readers follow a paragraph through what each sentence starts with.
activities.rationale: Makes thematic progression (Daneš, 1974) visible and actionable, following the old-to-new advice in Swales and Feak (2012).

activities.title: Connector diet
learnerActions: Remove all sentence-initial connectors from a paragraph
Reinsert only those that state a relation the reader could not otherwise infer
Compare readability with the original
activities.intendedInsight: Too many connectors can obscure the logic rather than clarify it.
activities.rationale: Responds to evidence that density of explicit cohesive devices is not a marker of better L2 writing (Crossley & McNamara, 2012).

difficulties.pattern: ‘Using lots of linking words makes my writing coherent.’
difficulties.revealedBy: Most sentences begin with a connector; mismatched relations (‘Moreover’ introducing a contrast).
difficulties.response: Teach logical ordering and given–new first, then precise connector choice. Do not reward connector counts in feedback or rubrics.

difficulties.pattern: Each sentence introduces a new topic in subject position, so the paragraph reads like a list.
difficulties.revealedBy: Readers cannot summarise the paragraph; few backward references.
difficulties.response: Use theme tracking and rewrite sentence openings so that each starts from given information.

diagnostic.task: Give five shuffled sentences from one paragraph and ask for the original order with reasons.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Correct order justified by reference, given–new information and logical relations.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Correct order justified mainly by the connectors.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Order based on content guesses only; no reasons given.

guidance.contextNotes: Foundation learners need basic reference and ordering. Pre-sessional and undergraduate in-sessional learners benefit from given–new and theme work on their own drafts. PGT writers' coherence problems often stem from dense information packaging; link to reg.information-density.
reviewNotes: Overlaps with coh.thematic-progression and coh.given-new; this topic applies them to paragraph construction and repair.

guidance.summary: Closing sentences are often where writers make the analytic move markers look for: saying what the evidence means. Present them functionally (significance, qualification, transition) rather than as a required restatement, and use authentic paragraphs, which often end on evidence or comment without a separate closing formula (a practitioner observation; Swales and Feak (2012) supply model paragraphs for analysis). This links to Wingate's (2012) emphasis on keeping the argument visible throughout a text.

activities.title: So what?
learnerActions: Read paragraphs that end on a piece of evidence
Add a final sentence answering ‘so what does this show for the question?’
Compare versions and choose the one that adds most
activities.intendedInsight: The best closing sentences add interpretation, not repetition.
activities.rationale: Prompts learners to state the link between evidence and argument which Wingate (2012) treats as part of developing a position through analysis of sources.

activities.title: Close or connect?
learnerActions: For each paragraph in a three-paragraph sequence, decide whether to close it, link it forward or leave it as it is
Justify the choices in pairs
activities.intendedInsight: A closing sentence is a choice determined by the paragraph's function.
activities.rationale: Encourages functional judgement rather than formula.

difficulties.pattern: Closing sentences that repeat the topic sentence in different words (‘Therefore, X is important’).
difficulties.revealedBy: Paragraphs that end where they began; no development of the point.
difficulties.response: Ask for one new element in the last sentence: an implication, a limitation or a link to the question.

difficulties.pattern: Overstated closings (‘This proves that…’) after limited evidence.
difficulties.revealedBy: Boosters clustered at paragraph ends.
difficulties.response: Link to hedging and claim calibration and ask learners to match the closing claim to the evidence given.

diagnostic.task: Give two consecutive paragraphs and ask for a closing sentence for the first that also prepares for the second.
diagnostic.strongResponse: The closing states the significance of the first paragraph and sets up its relation to the next point.
diagnostic.partialResponse: The closing either summarises or links, but not both.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Restates the topic sentence.

guidance.contextNotes: Foundation learners can use closing sentences routinely. From late pre-sessional stages, the emphasis moves to deciding when a closing is needed and to stating significance, which connects to criticality.
reviewNotes: Research on paragraph-concluding sentences specifically is limited; this guidance is practitioner-derived.

guidance.summary: There is no universally correct paragraph length; Braddock's (1974) study of professional prose suggests that paragraphing in practice is more varied than textbook rules imply. Teach division as a reader-oriented decision tied to shifts in point and function, and show variation across genres (shorter paragraphs in reports and online writing, longer ones in many humanities essays). In student essays, single-sentence paragraphs usually signal undeveloped ideas, and very long paragraphs usually contain more than one point.

activities.title: Where would you break?
learnerActions: Mark possible paragraph breaks in an unparagraphed text
Compare with the original and discuss the differences
Separate breaks required by a change of point from optional breaks made for readability
activities.intendedInsight: Some breaks are required by the content; others are judgements about readability.
activities.rationale: Makes paragraphing a reasoned decision, consistent with evidence of variation in expert texts (Braddock, 1974).

activities.title: Genre comparison
learnerActions: Estimate average paragraph length in an essay, a report and a blog post on the same topic
Explain the differences in terms of reader, purpose and medium
activities.intendedInsight: Paragraph-length conventions depend on genre and medium.
activities.rationale: Links paragraphing to audience and purpose rather than to a fixed rule.

difficulties.pattern: A new single-sentence paragraph for every point, as in journalistic or online writing.
difficulties.revealedBy: Many very short paragraphs; points asserted without support.
difficulties.response: Ask learners to develop each short paragraph (see par.support) or merge it with a related one, and show that development is what markers reward.

difficulties.pattern: Page-long paragraphs containing several points, sometimes reflecting paragraphing conventions learned in other languages or educational settings.
difficulties.revealedBy: Paragraphs of 300 words or more in which readers lose track.
difficulties.response: Reverse-outline the paragraph to locate shifts in point and divide there; present the English convention as a reader-oriented choice rather than as correcting a deficit.

diagnostic.task: Ask the learner to paragraph an unparagraphed 400-word text.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Breaks at shifts in point, paragraphs of workable length, and a clear justification for any optional break.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Mostly reasonable breaks, but one is driven by length and splits a point.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Breaks at fixed sentence counts, or none at all.

guidance.contextNotes: Foundation and pre-sessional teaching establishes defaults. In-sessional undergraduates need to see disciplinary and genre variation, including reports and online genres.
reviewNotes: Numerical guidance on ‘ideal’ paragraph length is deliberately avoided because it varies across genres and disciplines.

guidance.summary: Bruce (2008) distinguishes social genres, such as the essay, from cognitive genres, such as explanation and discussion, which organise stretches of text within them; paragraphs are often the unit at which these shift. Teaching paragraph functions helps learners see why introductions and conclusions are organised differently from body paragraphs and why counter-argument paragraphs need a response move. Swales and Feak (2012) provide accessible analyses of how stretches of text are organised for particular purposes.

activities.title: Function sort
learnerActions: Label the paragraphs of a model essay by function
Note the typical moves within each function
Use the notes to plan a new essay
activities.intendedInsight: Paragraphs with different functions have different internal structures.
activities.rationale: Function-based analysis applies genre-based thinking at paragraph level (Bruce, 2008).

activities.title: Write the bridge
learnerActions: Read the end of one section and the start of the next in an essay from which the transition has been removed
Write a short transitional paragraph
Compare with the original writer's solution
activities.intendedInsight: Transitional paragraphs help readers follow a longer argument.
activities.rationale: Prepares learners for longer texts in which transitions between sections matter.

difficulties.pattern: Introductions that launch straight into the first argument, or conclusions that introduce new evidence.
difficulties.revealedBy: Essays without context or without synthesis at the end.
difficulties.response: Analyse the typical moves of introductory and concluding paragraphs in exemplars before learners write their own.

difficulties.pattern: Counter-argument paragraphs that present the opposing view and then stop.
difficulties.revealedBy: Essays that appear to undermine their own thesis.
difficulties.response: Teach the response move (concession followed by rebuttal or qualification) as part of the counter-argument function.

diagnostic.task: Ask learners to label the function of six paragraphs from an essay and say what each one does.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Accurate labels, with the typical moves of each function described.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Identifies introduction and conclusion, but not transitional or counter-argument functions.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Labels paragraphs by topic only.

guidance.contextNotes: Foundation learners focus on introduction, body and conclusion. Pre-sessional learners add counter-argument and transitional functions, which become more important as texts lengthen (see coh.paragraph-transitions).

guidance.summary: Hyland (1999) shows that citation is a rhetorical choice through which writers position themselves in a disciplinary conversation, and Petrić (2007) found that higher-rated master's theses used citations for a wider range of functions, including evaluation and linking, than lower-rated ones. Pecorari (2013) argues that good source use needs to be taught explicitly rather than policed. Teach introduce–cite–comment as a default sequence, paying particular attention to the commentary sentences learners most often omit.

activities.title: Who is speaking?
learnerActions: Highlight the sentences of a source-based paragraph by voice: writer, source, or unclear
Identify where the reader cannot tell whose view is being expressed
Revise with signal phrases and comment sentences
activities.intendedInsight: Readers need to be able to track who is responsible for each claim.
activities.rationale: Builds the awareness of attribution that underpins acceptable source use (Pecorari, 2013).

activities.title: Add the comment
learnerActions: Take a paragraph that ends with a citation
Write a comment that evaluates, explains or connects the evidence
Compare comments and rank them by analytic value
activities.intendedInsight: The comment is where the writer's contribution lies.
activities.rationale: Higher-rated theses used citations for evaluation and linking more often than lower-rated ones (Petrić, 2007).

difficulties.pattern: Paragraphs that are strings of source summaries (‘A says… B says… C says…’).
difficulties.revealedBy: No claims of the writer's own; tutor comments such as ‘where is your voice?’.
difficulties.response: Require a writer's claim at the start and a comment after each piece of evidence; use short synthesis tasks.

difficulties.pattern: Not marking where a paraphrase ends, so later sentences could belong either to the writer or to the source.
difficulties.revealedBy: Ambiguous attribution; possible plagiarism concerns.
difficulties.response: Teach signal phrases at the boundaries of attributed content and the ‘who is speaking?’ check.

difficulties.pattern: Avoiding commentary because evaluating published authors feels presumptuous.
difficulties.revealedBy: Neutral reporting with no evaluation, even where the task asks for it.
difficulties.response: Show mitigated evaluative language and examples of what markers reward. Treat this as an expectation to make explicit, not as a trait of any group of learners.

diagnostic.task: Give two short source extracts and a claim and ask for a paragraph supporting the claim.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Claim first; both sources paraphrased and attributed; their relationship stated; a comment links the evidence back to the claim.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Claim and sources present, but commentary is minimal or attribution boundaries are unclear.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Sources summarised in sequence with no claim or comment, or copied.

guidance.contextNotes: Foundation learners need basic signal phrases and paragraphs built on a single source. Pre-sessional programmes should make integration central to extended writing. In-sessional undergraduates and PGT writers need disciplinary citation practices and paragraphs that put several sources in dialogue (see syn.synthesis-paragraphs).
reviewNotes: Overlaps with src.integrating-quotations and src.voice-boundaries; this topic covers the paragraph-level organisation of sources around the writer's point.

guidance.summary: Flower and Hayes (1981) model composing as goal-directed sub-processes (planning, translating, reviewing) that interrupt one another; Bereiter and Scardamalia (1987) add the contrast between knowledge-telling and knowledge-transforming, which maps closely onto tutors' complaints about ‘description’. Zamel's (1983) case studies suggest that skilled ESL writers, like skilled L1 writers, defer editing and revise for meaning. Teach the model through learners' own process data rather than as a diagram to memorise, and do not present it as a fixed sequence of stages.

activities.title: Process retrospective timeline
learnerActions: Reconstruct as precisely as possible how a recent short text was written, marking each episode as planning, drafting, reviewing or reading
Compare timelines in pairs and identify where each writer looped back and where they stayed linear
Annotate one point where an idea changed during drafting and say what triggered the change
activities.intendedInsight: Writing is not a pipeline; returning to planning mid-draft is normal and productive, not a sign of poor preparation.
activities.rationale: Making tacit process visible lets learners compare their behaviour with descriptions of recursive composing by skilled writers (Flower & Hayes, 1981; Zamel, 1983) without imposing a model as a rule.

activities.title: Telling versus transforming
learnerActions: Read two short responses to the same question: one listing recalled facts in the order remembered, one selecting and reordering them around a claim
Highlight the sentences in each that answer the question directly
Rewrite the opening of the first response so that its content serves a claim
activities.intendedInsight: The difference between the texts lies in what the writer did with their knowledge, not in how much they knew or how accurate the English is.
activities.rationale: Bereiter and Scardamalia's (1987) distinction gives teachers and learners shared language for the move from description to argument; contrasting texts keeps attention on observable textual consequences.

difficulties.pattern: ‘I should plan everything first and then just write it out; if I change my plan, I planned badly.’
difficulties.revealedBy: Outlines followed rigidly even when drafting exposes a weak point; reluctance to restructure; distress when the argument shifts.
difficulties.response: Normalise plan revision by showing real draft histories (your own or published ones) and ask for a short ‘what changed since my plan’ note with each draft. Do not penalise justified departures from a submitted outline.

difficulties.pattern: Writers stop after every sentence to check grammar and vocabulary and lose the thread of their argument.
difficulties.revealedBy: Very slow drafting, short texts with few ideas but relatively few errors, constant dictionary or translator use mid-sentence.
difficulties.response: Teach placeholders (for example [?word]) and timed drafting with editing explicitly postponed. Do not respond with more detailed grammar correction at the drafting stage, which reinforces premature editing.

diagnostic.task: Give learners an essay question and ten minutes. Every two minutes they note what they are doing (thinking, noting, writing, rereading, correcting).
diagnostic.strongResponse: The log alternates between planning, writing and rereading; at least one reread leads to a change of content or order; correction is mostly deferred.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Some planning before writing, but rereading is only for errors and the content order is fixed from the first line.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Writing starts immediately with no plan, or the whole period is spent planning; reviewing consists only of spelling and grammar checks.

guidance.contextNotes: At foundation and pre-sessional level, use the model to legitimise drafting and redrafting within portfolio or process-based assessment. In-sessional undergraduates benefit from relating it to their own assignment habits and deadlines. For postgraduates and doctoral researchers, emphasise knowledge-transforming and writing as a way of thinking (Kamler & Thomson, 2014), including the cost of postponing writing until the reading is ‘finished’.
reviewNotes: Cognitive process models were developed mainly with L1 writers. Their application to B1 writers is supported in general terms by L2 composing studies, but the heavier language-processing load at lower levels may make recursive composing harder to sustain.

guidance.summary: Flower and Hayes (1981) place the writer's representation of the rhetorical problem at the start of composing; a weak representation constrains everything that follows. Lea and Street (1998) show that tutors' expectations are often tacit, so task analysis should cover the implicit requirements of genre and discipline as well as the explicit wording. Use authentic briefs from learners' target departments where possible (Horowitz, 1986, documents the range of tasks set), and treat command words as cues to interpret in context rather than as fixed definitions.

activities.title: Brief deconstruction
learnerActions: Annotate a real assignment brief in four colours: instruction, topic, limits and other requirements
Rewrite the task as one sentence beginning ‘My text must…’
Compare with a partner, list the remaining ambiguities and draft a short email asking a tutor about one of them
activities.intendedInsight: A brief contains more instructions than the question line, and some requirements are implicit.
activities.rationale: Explicit task representation is the first planning operation in cognitive models (Flower & Hayes, 1981), and authentic briefs expose the task types learners will actually meet (Horowitz, 1986).

activities.title: Same topic, different task
learnerActions: Read three questions on the same topic with different command words and limiting conditions
Sketch the main point a strong answer to each would make
Explain why one paragraph of content could be relevant to one question but not to another
activities.intendedInsight: Relevance is defined by the task, not by the topic.
activities.rationale: Contrasting tasks that share a topic makes the effect of the instruction visible and counters topic-driven knowledge-telling (Bereiter & Scardamalia, 1987).

difficulties.pattern: Learners write everything they know about the topic and overlook the command word or a limiting condition such as a period or context.
