difficulties.revealedBy: Accurate but generic essays; tutor comments such as ‘not focused on the question’.
difficulties.response: Require a one-sentence task statement before planning and check plans against it. Rather than handing out a list of command-word definitions, have learners infer what a command word demands from high- and low-scoring answers.

difficulties.pattern: ‘Discuss means describe both sides; critically evaluate means criticise.’
difficulties.revealedBy: Balanced lists with no conclusion; wholly negative evaluations.
difficulties.response: Compare answers to the same command word that received different marks and have learners articulate the difference; stress that most command words require a reasoned judgement.

difficulties.pattern: Assuming that asking a tutor to clarify a brief is impolite or will be judged negatively.
difficulties.revealedBy: Questions about the brief surface only after submission; optional elements misinterpreted.
difficulties.response: Model appropriate clarification requests and discuss when tutors expect them, linking to email and office-hour conventions.

diagnostic.task: Give a brief containing a question, a word limit, required reading and a three-criterion rubric. Ask for a list of everything the assignment requires, in five minutes.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Identifies instruction, topic, limits, genre, required sources and at least one implication of the criteria (for example that ‘critical analysis’ requires evaluation, not description).
diagnostic.partialResponse: Identifies topic and word limit but misses limiting conditions or the implications of the criteria.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Restates the topic only, or lists generic study advice unrelated to the brief.

guidance.contextNotes: Foundation and pre-sessional teaching can start with adapted briefs but should move quickly to authentic ones. In-sessional work is most effective when learners bring their own module briefs. At PGT level briefs are often shorter and more open, so the emphasis shifts to defining scope and choosing an angle. Test preparation can foster a narrow view of writing tasks (Moore & Morton, 2005), which may need explicit unlearning.
reviewNotes: Overlaps with voc.command-words (lexical meaning of command words) and exm.question-analysis (exam questions and time allocation); this topic covers representation of the whole brief.

guidance.summary: In Flower and Hayes's (1981) model, generating is a sub-process of planning that retrieves content from memory and the task environment; Bereiter and Scardamalia (1987) show that novice writers tend to stop at whatever first comes to mind. Present techniques as options to try rather than a required sequence, and always follow generation with task-based selection. Freewriting (Elbow, 1973) suits writers who censor themselves; question heuristics suit those who produce little. Allow generation in any language.

activities.title: Heuristic ladder
learnerActions: Write one obvious point in answer to a question
Apply five questions to it (why, how, when does it not hold, who disagrees, so what) and note an answer to each
Mark which answers need evidence from reading
activities.intendedInsight: Interrogating a first idea is often more productive than searching for more first ideas.
activities.rationale: Structured prompts act as procedural facilitation, the kind of support Bereiter and Scardamalia (1987) used to help novice writers reach beyond knowledge-telling.

activities.title: Generate, then judge
learnerActions: Freewrite for five minutes on the question without stopping or correcting
Underline phrases that could become points
Sort the points into relevant, possibly relevant and off-task, using the task statement
activities.intendedInsight: Postponing judgement produces more material; selection is a separate, task-driven step.
activities.rationale: Freewriting separates production from evaluation (Elbow, 1973); pairing it with task-based selection stops it becoming unfocused.

difficulties.pattern: ‘I have no ideas about this topic.’
difficulties.revealedBy: Blank pages, very short plans, requests for model answers.
difficulties.response: Start from talk or questions rather than writing, allow L1 notes, and give a short reading to prime content. Do not supply the ideas yourself, which builds dependence.

difficulties.pattern: Generates many ideas but keeps all of them, producing list-like plans.
difficulties.revealedBy: Plans with eight or more unconnected points for a 1,000-word text.
difficulties.response: Require explicit selection against the task statement, with a reason for each discarded idea.

diagnostic.task: Give a question and ask for a three-minute brainstorm, then the three best points with a reason for each choice.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Ten or more varied ideas, including at least one non-obvious angle; choices justified by the question.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Several ideas but similar in kind; choices justified by preference (‘easier to write about’).
diagnostic.gapResponse: Two or three ideas that restate the question; no selection rationale.

guidance.contextNotes: At foundation level, generation is often the main bottleneck and benefits from oral rehearsal and shared brainstorming. Pre-sessional and in-sessional writers increasingly generate from reading, so link generation to reading questions. For postgraduates, generative writing and discussing ideas with peers or supervisors are usually more useful than formal brainstorming.
reviewNotes: Mind mapping is widely recommended, but research on concept maps concerns learning from maps rather than idea generation for writing, so it is not cited here as support.

guidance.summary: Planning in Flower and Hayes's (1981) model includes organising and goal-setting as well as generating. Ellis and Yuan (2004) found that pre-task planning time increased the fluency and syntactic complexity of L2 writing, although their task was narrative and transfer to source-based academic writing is an inference. Teach outlines whose entries are claims, so that the plan already carries the argument, and treat every outline as provisional (Hyland, 2003).

activities.title: Topic labels to claims
learnerActions: Take an outline made of topic labels (‘1 Background, 2 Advantages, 3 Disadvantages’)
Rewrite each entry as a full-sentence claim that helps answer the question
Read the claims in sequence and check that they form an argument without the body text
activities.intendedInsight: An outline made of claims is already a draft of the argument; one made of topics is only a table of contents.
activities.rationale: Making each plan entry a claim turns topic-driven planning into goal-driven planning of the kind associated with expert writers (Flower & Hayes, 1981; Bereiter & Scardamalia, 1987).

activities.title: Format trial
learnerActions: Plan the same question once as a linear outline and once as a map or table
Draft one paragraph from each plan
Note which format exposed missing links or evidence
activities.intendedInsight: Different formats reveal different weaknesses; there is no single correct planning format.
activities.rationale: Offering formats as tools to compare supports learner choice without relying on unsupported learning-styles claims.

difficulties.pattern: Plans are lists of topics copied from lecture headings or source sections.
difficulties.revealedBy: Outlines consisting of nouns only; essays that describe each topic in turn.
difficulties.response: Require claim-based outlines and model converting topics into claims by asking ‘so what does this section show?’ for each entry.

difficulties.pattern: ‘Planning wastes time when the deadline is close or in an exam.’
difficulties.revealedBy: No visible plan; essays that drift or end without a conclusion.
difficulties.response: Practise five-minute plans and compare the resulting texts with unplanned ones. Do not insist on elaborate plans for every task; brief plans are legitimate.

diagnostic.task: Give a question, a set of source notes and ten minutes to produce an outline.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Claim-based outline with evidence attached to each point, a stated ordering logic and rough word allocations.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Logical sequence with evidence attached, but entries are topics rather than claims.
diagnostic.gapResponse: List of loosely related topics, or the notes reproduced in source order.

guidance.contextNotes: Foundation learners benefit from template outlines that are gradually withdrawn. Pre-sessional extended writing is a good place to teach outlines revised alongside drafts and submitted for feedback. At PGT and PGR level, planning extends to chapter and section maps negotiated with supervisors; in timed exams, plans become brief but remain claim-based.
reviewNotes: Ellis and Yuan (2004) used a narrative writing task; the effects of planning time on extended, source-based academic writing are extrapolated.

guidance.summary: Zamel (1983) observed that more skilled ESL writers deferred attention to surface form and explored ideas while drafting, and Sommers (1980) found that experienced writers used drafting and redrafting to discover what they meant. In translating ideas into language (Flower & Hayes, 1981), L2 writers carry a heavier linguistic load, so strategies that protect momentum—placeholders, L1 notes, timed drafting—are especially useful. Present drafting as producing complete, revisable text, not as careless writing.

activities.title: Placeholder drafting
learnerActions: Draft for 20 minutes from a plan, writing [REF], [WORD?] or [CHECK] instead of stopping
Count placeholders and words produced
Resolve the placeholders in a separate session and compare the time spent
activities.intendedInsight: Separating getting ideas down from getting them right is faster and produces more content.
activities.rationale: Deferring local concerns mirrors the behaviour of skilled L2 writers described by Zamel (1983) and reduces competition for attention during translating (Flower & Hayes, 1981).

activities.title: What changed while drafting?
learnerActions: Reread the plan and the draft side by side
Mark one place where the draft says something the plan did not
Decide whether the change improves the answer and update the plan
activities.intendedInsight: Drafting is a way of discovering and testing the argument, not just transcribing a plan.
activities.rationale: Sommers (1980) associates experienced writers' revision with discovering meaning through drafting; making this explicit legitimises changes to the plan.

difficulties.pattern: ‘My first sentence has to be perfect before I can go on.’
difficulties.revealedBy: Long time spent on introductions, many deleted openings, incomplete drafts.
difficulties.response: Start drafting with the easiest body paragraph and write the introduction last. Do not give detailed language feedback on early drafts, which reinforces perfectionism.

difficulties.pattern: Composing each sentence in the first language and translating it word by word carries L1 clause structure and collocation into the English text.
difficulties.revealedBy: Sentences that are locally grammatical but hard to parse; collocations that mirror L1 patterns; heavy translator use.
difficulties.response: Encourage the L1 for notes and planning, but draft in English from those notes (see wpr.l1-in-composing). Do not ban other languages outright, which usually drives the practice underground.

diagnostic.task: Ask learners to draft 300 words in 20 minutes from a supplied outline and then write two sentences about how they worked.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Complete draft following the plan, with placeholders and at least one noted development of the argument.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Complete draft but with long pauses for correction, or an incomplete draft with polished early paragraphs.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Introduction only, heavily reworked; reports being unable to continue until it was right.

guidance.contextNotes: At foundation level, scaffold with paragraph-by-paragraph drafting from detailed plans. On pre-sessional programmes, draft deadlines within extended projects make drafting visible and give an opportunity for content-focused feedback. Postgraduates often over-read before drafting; encourage early, low-stakes drafting of more descriptive sections such as methods or background.

guidance.summary: Spivey (1990) describes writing from sources as discourse synthesis involving selecting, organising and connecting content. Plakans (2008) found that composing processes differed between reading-to-write and writing-only tasks, with source-based tasks prompting more interaction between reading and writing for many writers. Grabe and Zhang (2013) and Hirvela (2004) argue that EAP should teach reading and writing together. Teach the transition from notes to text explicitly, including note formats that separate source content from the writer's own comments.

activities.title: Notes to paragraph, sources closed
learnerActions: Make two-column notes from two short sources: source content on the left, own reactions and questions on the right
Close the sources and write a paragraph making one point, using both columns
Check the paragraph against the sources for accuracy and attribution only after writing
activities.intendedInsight: Writing from notes rather than from the source supports transformation and reduces close copying.
activities.rationale: Separating source content and personal response at the note stage prepares the connecting operation of discourse synthesis (Spivey, 1990).

activities.title: Reorganise, don't summarise in order
learnerActions: Receive short summaries of three sources
Cut them into points and regroup the points under two claims that answer a question
Write a topic sentence for each group
activities.intendedInsight: Source content should be arranged by the writer's points, not by source.
activities.rationale: Organising is the operation that distinguishes synthesis from serial summary (Spivey, 1990) and benefits from integrated reading–writing instruction (Grabe & Zhang, 2013).

difficulties.pattern: Writing with the source open and composing sentence by sentence from it.
difficulties.revealedBy: Patchwritten passages, source-order organisation, little or no commentary.
difficulties.response: Teach close-the-source drafting from notes, and treat patchwriting first as a developmental stage to be moved beyond rather than as misconduct.

difficulties.pattern: ‘The more sources I include, the more academic my essay is.’
difficulties.revealedBy: Sources piled up with no link to the point; reporting verbs carrying the whole argument.
difficulties.response: Ask for a one-line justification of each source's role in the paragraph, and limit sources per point in practice tasks.

diagnostic.task: Give a short source and a question and ask for one paragraph that uses the source to support a point of the learner's own.
diagnostic.strongResponse: The learner's point leads; source content is selected, paraphrased and attributed; a comment links the evidence to the point.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Accurate, attributed summary of the source, but no point of the learner's own or no comment.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Copied or closely patchwritten source sentences, missing attribution, or no link to the question.

guidance.contextNotes: Foundation and pre-sessional programmes should build reading-to-write tasks into assessment, since many proficiency tests ask for writing from personal knowledge (Moore & Morton, 2005). In-sessional learners need help applying the process to longer, denser disciplinary readings. At PGT level the emphasis moves to organising large reading loads around a focused argument.
reviewNotes: Overlaps with syn.integrated-tasks and rdc.reading-for-writing; this topic focuses on the composing transition from notes to the writer's own text.

guidance.summary: Johns (1997) argues for a socioliterate approach in which learners study how texts are shaped by roles and contexts, and Hyland (2005) shows that academic writing is interactive, with writers anticipating readers' needs and objections. The assessed essay's double audience—an expert marker addressed as if an informed peer—is a tacit convention that, as Lea and Street (1998) show, is rarely explained. Make the reader explicit in every task and compare how the same content changes for different readers.

activities.title: Same content, three readers
learnerActions: Write two sentences on one topic for a younger student, an expert marker and a newspaper reader
Compare what each version explains, assumes and argues
List three features that mark the version written for the marker
activities.intendedInsight: Expert readers expect explicit reasoning and a position, not more basic explanation.
activities.rationale: Varying the reader while holding content constant isolates audience effects, in line with a socioliterate approach (Johns, 1997).

activities.title: Reader questions
learnerActions: Exchange a paragraph with a partner, who writes the question an expert reader would ask after each sentence
Revise to answer the most important unanswered question in the text
activities.intendedInsight: Academic writing anticipates and answers a reader's questions.
activities.rationale: Treating text as a dialogue with an imagined reader reflects interactional accounts of written discourse (Hoey, 2001; Hyland, 2005).

difficulties.pattern: ‘The teacher already knows this, so I don't need to explain it.’
difficulties.revealedBy: Undefined key terms, skipped reasoning steps, tutor comments such as ‘explain’ or ‘how?’.
difficulties.response: Explain the convention of writing for an informed reader who is checking the writer's understanding, and show annotated feedback on such gaps.

difficulties.pattern: Treating the marker as an authority to agree with or impress with elaborate vocabulary.
difficulties.revealedBy: Lecture views reproduced without evaluation; inflated register.
difficulties.response: Discuss what markers reward using criteria and exemplars, and reframe the task as offering a reasoned view to an informed reader.

diagnostic.task: Ask the learner to identify the reader and purpose of three briefs (an essay, a reflective log, a policy brief) and name one way each affects the writing.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Distinguishes readers and purposes and names concrete consequences for content, explicitness and register.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Identifies the readers but gives generic consequences (‘be formal’).
diagnostic.gapResponse: Treats all three as written for ‘the teacher’ with the same purpose of showing knowledge.

guidance.contextNotes: Foundation learners need the marker-as-reader convention made explicit early. In-sessional undergraduates meet a wider range of readers through professional and public-facing genres. PGT writers increasingly write for specialist peers and practitioners, so audience analysis becomes part of choosing and shaping genres.

guidance.summary: Self-regulated learning models (Zimmerman, 2002) highlight forethought, performance monitoring and self-reflection, all of which extended writing demands. Thesis-writing guidance (Paltridge & Starfield, 2020) and structured writing programmes such as Belcher's (2019) recommend regular writing, staged goals and planned feedback over last-minute bursts. Teach planning tools in the context of a real project and review progress at intervals; plans that are never revisited achieve little.

activities.title: Backward plan with a word budget
learnerActions: Work back from the deadline to set dated milestones, including feedback and editing
Allocate words to each section of the project
Share the plan with a peer who checks for unrealistic weeks and missing contingency
activities.intendedInsight: Revision and feedback need protected time that must be scheduled before drafting starts.
activities.rationale: Explicit forethought and goal-setting form the first phase of self-regulation (Zimmerman, 2002).

activities.title: Writing log
learnerActions: Record date, time spent, words or sections produced and obstacles after each writing session for three weeks
Review the log to identify productive times and conditions
Set one routine change for the following fortnight
activities.intendedInsight: Regular short sessions often produce more than occasional long ones, and patterns only become visible when recorded.
activities.rationale: Monitoring and reflection complete the self-regulation cycle (Zimmerman, 2002), and regular writing is central to structured article-writing guidance (Belcher, 2019).

difficulties.pattern: Postponing all writing until the reading feels complete.
difficulties.revealedBy: No drafts until the final weeks; long reading lists with few notes.
difficulties.response: Set early, low-stakes writing milestones, such as a summary of key sources or a draft methods section, and revisit drafting as a way of thinking (see wpr.drafting).

difficulties.pattern: Schedules that assume every week will be equally productive.
difficulties.revealedBy: Repeated slippage; plans abandoned after the first missed milestone.
difficulties.response: Build in contingency weeks and review the plan every fortnight, treating replanning as normal rather than as failure.

diagnostic.task: Ask for a schedule and word budget for a 3,000-word assignment due in four weeks alongside two other deadlines.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Dated milestones, a word budget by section, time for feedback and editing, and explicit handling of competing deadlines.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Milestones present but no word budget, or no time reserved for revision.
diagnostic.gapResponse: A single deadline with a plan to ‘write it in the last week’.

guidance.contextNotes: Pre-sessional extended projects are often learners' first long text and a useful rehearsal. Undergraduate and PGT dissertations compress project management into a few months alongside taught modules. For PGR, management spans years and links to supervision, writing groups and publication planning (see res.writing-productivity).
reviewNotes: Overlaps with res.writing-productivity, which addresses doctoral routines; this topic covers generic project management from pre-sessional level upwards.

guidance.summary: Rose (1980) found that blocked student writers often held rigid rules and inflexible plans, whereas fluent writers used flexible heuristics. Freewriting (Elbow, 1973) lowers the stakes of producing text, and doctoral writing pedagogy treats writing difficulty as bound up with identity and authority as well as technique (Kamler & Thomson, 2014). Treat blocks as normal and solvable, match strategies to likely causes, and avoid framing them as purely a matter of motivation.

activities.title: Rule audit
learnerActions: List the writing rules you follow (for example ‘always write the introduction first’ or ‘never use I’)
Classify each as an absolute rule or a flexible guideline, and look for counter-examples in published writing in your field
Rewrite unhelpful absolute rules as heuristics
activities.intendedInsight: Some blocks come from rules that are not actually requirements.
activities.rationale: Rose (1980) linked blocking to rigid rules; testing rules against real texts also counters widespread style myths.

activities.title: Ten-minute starts
learnerActions: Freewrite for ten minutes, in any language, about what you want the stuck section to say
Extract one sentence that could open the section
Set a concrete goal for the next ten-minute session
activities.intendedInsight: Producing imperfect text is usually the quickest way out of a block.
activities.rationale: Freewriting removes evaluation from initial production (Elbow, 1973).

difficulties.pattern: ‘I can't start writing until I know exactly what I think.’
difficulties.revealedBy: Extended reading and note-making with no drafts.
difficulties.response: Present writing as a way of finding out what one thinks and set exploratory writing that is not assessed.

difficulties.pattern: ‘My English isn't good enough, so whatever I write will be wrong.’
difficulties.revealedBy: Avoidance, missed draft deadlines, very short drafts, apologetic notes to the tutor.
difficulties.response: Separate content feedback from language feedback on early drafts and normalise multilingual drafting. Do not respond with intensive error correction on early work, which confirms the fear.

diagnostic.task: Ask the learner to describe the last time they could not write and what they did about it.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Names a specific cause and a strategy that addressed it, and identifies what they would do next time.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Describes the feeling but uses only generic strategies (waiting, more reading).
diagnostic.gapResponse: Treats the block as a fixed trait (‘I'm just a bad writer’) and has no strategies.

guidance.contextNotes: Pre-sessional and first-year undergraduates often block on high-stakes first assignments; postgraduates and doctoral researchers more often on long, ill-defined sections. At PGR level, writing groups and retreats provide useful structures, and a persistent block may signal an unresolved conceptual problem worth raising with supervisors.
reviewNotes: Rose (1980) is a small-sample study of L1 undergraduates; its extension to L2 writers is plausible but not directly tested.

guidance.summary: Studies of L2 composing show that writers use the L1 for particular sub-processes, especially planning and generating ideas, and that L1 use tends to decrease as L2 proficiency rises (Wang & Wen, 2002). Cumming (1989) found that writing expertise and L2 proficiency make separate contributions to L2 writing, so composing expertise developed in another language is a resource. Translanguaging perspectives (García & Li Wei, 2014) legitimise plurilingual composing. Lee (2020) reports that EFL students who used machine-translation output as a reference while revising reduced some errors, but full-text translation raises learning and integrity concerns, so rules need explicit discussion.

activities.title: Language map of my process
learnerActions: Record which language you used for each step of a recent piece of writing (reading, notes, planning, drafting, checking)
Compare with peers and discuss the benefits and risks at each step
Choose one change to try in the next assignment
activities.intendedInsight: Other languages are most useful for thinking and planning; drafting in English from those plans builds L2 composing fluency.
activities.rationale: Making language choice explicit turns habit into strategy, consistent with evidence that L1 use varies by composing activity (Wang & Wen, 2002).

activities.title: Plan in any language, draft in English
learnerActions: Plan a paragraph in your strongest language or a mixture of languages
Draft it in English without translating the plan line by line
Afterwards, check specific terms with a dictionary, corpus or (if permitted) machine translation
activities.intendedInsight: A plurilingual plan can support an English text that follows English academic patterns.
activities.rationale: Draws on the plurilingual repertoire as a resource (García & Li Wei, 2014) while limiting carry-over of L1 sentence structure.

difficulties.pattern: ‘Using my first language is cheating, or it will stop my English improving.’
difficulties.revealedBy: Difficulty generating ideas in English, thin content, guilt about L1 notes.
difficulties.response: Explain that L1 planning is common among successful L2 writers and discuss when it helps. Do not ban L1 use in planning activities.

difficulties.pattern: Writing the whole text in the L1, translating it with machine translation and lightly editing the output.
difficulties.revealedBy: Fluent but uneven text, unexpected term choices, a gap between in-class and take-home writing (which on its own is expected, since timed in-class writing is usually weaker, and is not evidence of translation or misconduct).
difficulties.response: Clarify local rules; discuss what the learner loses (practice, control of voice) and the integrity risks; show targeted uses of translation that are permitted.

difficulties.pattern: Translating clause by clause carries over L1 information order and clause chaining, producing very long or topic–comment sentences that are hard to parse in English.
difficulties.revealedBy: Sentences that are grammatical in parts but difficult to follow; unusual sentence boundaries.
difficulties.response: Draft in English from notes, then edit sentence boundaries and information order. Explain the mechanism in linguistic terms rather than attributing it to a ‘culture’.

diagnostic.task: Ask the learner to plan aloud, in any language(s), for a short question and then write the first paragraph in English.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Plans in whichever language is efficient; the English paragraph is drafted from the plan with English syntax and appropriate terms.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Plans in L1; the English paragraph closely translates plan sentences and contains awkward structures.
diagnostic.gapResponse: No plan; translates sentence by sentence or asks to use a translator for the whole paragraph.

guidance.contextNotes: Foundation learners rely most on the L1 and need explicit guidance on productive uses. Pre-sessional programmes should state rules on translation and AI tools clearly, as practice varies. Doctoral researchers often read and think in several languages; plurilingual note-making and the use of non-English sources are part of research practice (see src.multilingual-sources).
reviewNotes: Institutional rules on machine translation vary widely and change quickly; guidance here is deliberately non-prescriptive.
wangwen2002 and cumming1989 are proposed references pending verification.

guidance.summary: Word limits are task constraints that force prioritisation: under-length drafts usually lack analysis, and over-length ones usually contain description or repetition. Teach word budgeting at the planning stage and cutting as a revision decision before it becomes a sentence-level task, reflecting the distinction between global revision and local editing (Sommers, 1980). Conventions on what counts and on tolerances vary, so learners should check local regulations rather than rely on general rules.

activities.title: Word budget
learnerActions: Allocate a 2,000-word limit across the introduction, body sections and conclusion of a given plan
Justify the largest allocation
Compare the budget with the actual proportions of a high-scoring exemplar
activities.intendedInsight: Introductions and background usually need far fewer words than learners give them.
activities.rationale: Budgeting turns the limit into a planning tool and exposes over-weighted description early (Hyland, 2003).

activities.title: Cut by value
learnerActions: Rank the paragraphs of an over-length draft by their contribution to the argument
Remove or compress the lowest-ranked material
Only then tighten sentences, recording the words saved at each step
activities.intendedInsight: Structural cuts save more words and do less damage than trimming every sentence.
activities.rationale: Separating global from local cutting mirrors the distinction between revision and editing (Sommers, 1980).

difficulties.pattern: ‘Writing more shows that I know more.’
difficulties.revealedBy: Long background sections, repetition, persistently over-length drafts.
difficulties.response: Show marker comments on description and practise reducing background to one or two sentences.

difficulties.pattern: Cutting the commentary and keeping the source summaries.
difficulties.revealedBy: Shortened drafts that have become more descriptive.
difficulties.response: Highlight analysis sentences before cutting and protect them.

difficulties.pattern: Assuming that references and quotations never count, or that a fixed tolerance always applies.
difficulties.revealedBy: Length penalties and queries after marking.
difficulties.response: Have learners find and quote the local rule for each assignment as part of analysing the brief (see wpr.task-analysis).

diagnostic.task: Ask for a word budget for a 1,500-word essay with three body sections, and a plan for cutting a supplied 1,800-word draft by 300 words.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Budget favours the argument sections; the cutting plan removes low-value content first and protects analysis.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Reasonable budget, but the cutting plan trims sentences evenly throughout.
diagnostic.gapResponse: No budget; cuts the conclusion or the analysis.

guidance.contextNotes: Foundation and early pre-sessional learners more often struggle to reach limits and need help developing analysis. Undergraduates and PGT students more often overshoot, especially in reading-heavy assignments. Doctoral researchers deal with journal limits and thesis regulations, where cutting may mean moving material to appendices or other outputs.
reviewNotes: There is little dedicated research on managing word limits; guidance is practitioner-derived, and the citations support the general framing of task constraints and revision rather than specific techniques.

guidance.summary: Teach formatting as compliance with conventions the reader has specified rather than as a universal standard: style guides such as APA (American Psychological Association, 2020) and MLA (Modern Language Association of America, 2021) differ, and many departments impose their own templates. Combine brief instruction with hands-on practice in word-processing styles, and keep formatting in proportion to its weight in assessment.

activities.title: Style-sheet comparison
learnerActions: Compare the formatting requirements of two style guides or departmental handbooks and list five differences
Apply one set of requirements to a short document using built-in styles
activities.intendedInsight: Formatting conventions are local choices; the skill lies in finding the right one and applying it consistently.
activities.rationale: Comparing style guides counters the belief that there is one correct academic format.

activities.title: Pre-submission checklist
learnerActions: Build a formatting checklist from an assignment brief
Check a peer's document and then one's own against it
activities.intendedInsight: A checklist makes final checks quick and systematic and keeps them at the end of the process.
activities.rationale: Separating presentation checks from content work prevents formatting from displacing revision.

difficulties.pattern: Formatting manually with spaces, tabs and typed numbers, so the layout breaks whenever the text is edited.
difficulties.revealedBy: Inconsistent headings, broken numbering, misaligned text.
difficulties.response: Teach styles and automatic numbering briefly and check them in class.

difficulties.pattern: Spending disproportionate time on appearance at the expense of content.
difficulties.revealedBy: Heavily designed documents with weak argument.
difficulties.response: Show how marking criteria weight presentation and schedule formatting for the end of the process.

diagnostic.task: Ask the learner to identify the formatting requirements for a given assignment and apply them to a one-page draft.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Finds all stated requirements and applies them consistently using styles.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Applies most requirements, but manually and with some inconsistencies.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Unaware of the requirements; submits in default formatting.

guidance.contextNotes: Foundation learners may be new to academic word processing. Pre-sessional and in-sessional learners need department-specific conventions. At PGR level, thesis regulations and journal templates dominate, and document accessibility (see mmd.accessibility) becomes increasingly relevant.
reviewNotes: The scope note mentions headings; headings as a rhetorical choice in essays are covered by ess.headings.

authorNotes: edt.editing-tools overlaps substantially with dig.automated-feedback-tools and gai.language-support. I linked edt.editing-tools to gai.how-genai-works only, so the DIG and GAI authors can make their topics depend on edt.editing-tools or edt.grammar-editing without creating cycles.

edt.grammar-editing overlaps with grm.error-monitoring and fbk.corrective-feedback. I treat grm.error-monitoring as a hard prerequisite and deliberately did not link to fbk.corrective-feedback, to leave the FBK author free to choose the direction.

edt.criteria-self-assessment overlaps with fbk.self-peer-assessment, and edt.peer-review overlaps with it too. I avoided edges to fbk.self-peer-assessment for the same reason; one of the two self-assessment topics could perhaps be merged in a later revision.
edt.proofreading-ethics overlaps with int.collusion and gai.policies; there is no skeleton topic on literacy brokering and editorial support for doctoral writers beyond pub.multilingual-scholars.

No skeleton topic covers revising in response to tutor or supervisor feedback specifically (as opposed to fbk.acting-on-feedback in general or pub.responding-reviewers); a topic such as ‘revising from feedback’ would sit naturally in EDT.

ess.essay-types overlaps with the GES production topics and with ges.genre-families. Suggested division: ess.essay-types is the conceptual overview of essay purposes and is a natural prerequisite for ges.argumentative-essay, ges.discussion-essay, ges.compare-contrast-essay, ges.explanation-essay and ges.problem-solution-essay. I avoided any edge from ess.* to ges.* to keep this direction open.
ess.criticality overlaps with crt.description-analysis-evaluation and rdc.critical-response. I treat the CRT topic as the conceptual prerequisite and ess.criticality as its written realisation.
ess.headings overlaps with grp.report-conventions and wpr.formatting. I did not link to grp.report-conventions so that the report topic may depend on ess.headings if its author wishes.
ess.titles is not essay-specific (it covers reports, dissertations and articles); it might sit better in a cross-genre domain, or its scope note could be widened explicitly.
ess.answering-question overlaps with wpr.task-analysis; the distinction is that task analysis happens before writing, whereas answering the question is maintained during drafting and revision.
There is no skeleton topic for the exploratory or ‘delayed-thesis’ essay common in some humanities traditions; ess.thesis-statement notes it as a variant.

par.internal-coherence overlaps heavily with coh.thematic-progression, coh.given-new and coh.lexical-cohesion. I treat the COH topics as prerequisites (resources) and par.internal-coherence as their application to paragraph construction; COH authors should avoid edges from COH topics to par.* to prevent cycles.

par.integrating-evidence overlaps with src.integrating-quotations, src.voice-boundaries and syn.synthesis-paragraphs. I deliberately used sta.averral-attribution and src.signal-phrases rather than src.voice-boundaries as prerequisites so that src.voice-boundaries and syn.synthesis-paragraphs can depend on par.integrating-evidence if their authors wish.

par.paragraph-unit is linked to rds.main-ideas rather than rds.paragraph-structure-reading, so that the reading author can make rds.paragraph-structure-reading depend on par.paragraph-unit or vice versa without creating a cycle through my edges.

par.peel is a scaffold rather than a competence; it might sit better as a teaching note inside par.support, but it is retained because the skeleton fixes it and because many foundation programmes teach it explicitly.
par.concluding-sentences has thin research support; it might be merged with par.paragraph-functions in a later revision.

wpr.task-analysis overlaps with voc.command-words and exm.question-analysis. Suggested division: voc = meanings of command words; wpr = representation of a whole coursework brief, including criteria and implicit genre requirements; exm = timed exam questions and mark allocation. The fbk.marking-criteria topic should probably not list wpr.task-analysis as a prerequisite, because edt.criteria-self-assessment already depends on fbk.marking-criteria.

wpr.reading-to-write overlaps with rdc.reading-for-writing and syn.integrated-tasks. I have made rdc.reading-for-writing a prerequisite of wpr.reading-to-write; the reading and synthesis authors should avoid the reverse edge to prevent a cycle.

wpr.managing-long-projects overlaps with res.writing-productivity and lrn.time-management. I treat res.writing-productivity as the doctoral specialisation that could depend on wpr.managing-long-projects, not the reverse.

wpr.formatting's scope (headings, page layout, templates) overlaps with dig.word-processing (tool use) and ess.headings (rhetorical use of headings). I link wpr.formatting -> dig.word-processing (soft); the digital-literacy author should avoid the reverse edge.

wpr.l1-in-composing overlaps with dig.machine-translation and idn.plurilingual-repertoire. I deliberately did not make it depend on dig.machine-translation, so dig.machine-translation may depend on wpr.l1-in-composing if its author wishes.
No skeleton topic covers dictation or speech-to-text drafting and other assistive composing technologies; this could sit in DIG or here.
